articleTitle: A 1.2GS/s 11b Time-Interleaved SAR ADC with Low-Cost Derivative-Based Background Timing-Skew Calibration and Variable-Load Comparators
abstract: Time-interleaved (TI) SARs are popular choices for high-speed ADCs due to their high energy efficiency and scaling compatibility, but they suffer from timing skew that severely degrades the linearity. The key to the background calibration of the timing skew error $\Delta t$ is to correctly estimate its sign, so that $\Delta t$ can be minimized by adjusting a variable delay line. One way to estimate $\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta t)$ is to add a reference ADC channel (ref-ADC) and compare its output $\mathrm{D}_{\text {ref }}$ with each sub-ADC channel output $D_{i}$ to obtain $\Delta V_{i n}=D_{i}-D_{\text {ref. }}$. However, without knowing the input derivative dV in $/ \mathrm{dt}$, the estimation of $\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta t)$ relies on computing auto-correlation or variance, which takes millions or even billions of samples to converge [1]. Thus, it is preferred to extract both $\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\text {in }}$ and $\mathrm{d} \mathrm{V}_{\text {in }} / \mathrm{dt}$, which allows the direct solving of $\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta t)=\operatorname{sgn}\left(\Delta V_{i n} \cdot d V_{\text {in }} / d t\right)$ and achieves a fast convergence. The derivative can be estimated by using a digital FIR filter, but it is computationally intensive and limits the input bandwidth [2]. It can also be extracted by adding another channel to build an analog derivative filter [3] [4]. This approach supports wide input bandwidth, but two extra channels result in large area and power overhead. To minimize the cost, this paper proposes a novel timing-skew calibration technique that uses only one extra channel to extract both $\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\text {in }}$ and $\mathrm{d} \mathrm{V}_{\text {in }} / \mathrm{dt}$, achieving low-cost and fast calibration. Dummy loads are used to compensate the impedance modulation effect. This paper also proposes a novel variable-load comparator. It outperforms the conventional design in both speed and energy efficiency. Equipped with the proposed calibration technique and comparators, a prototype 1.2GS/s 11b TI SAR ADC with an on-chip timing-skew calibration engine achieves 58.4 dB SNDR while consuming only 4.6 mW, leading to a competitive FoMs of 169.6 dB and FoM w of $5.6 \mathrm{fJ} /$ conv-step.

articleTitle: A Fully Integrated 400MHz Band Transceiver with a 96Mbps 16QAM Transmitter and a Phase Tracking Receiver in 40-nm CMOS
abstract: The demand for low-power, high data-rate radios in biomedical applications, such as brain-machine interfaces and high-density neural signal recorders, has been on the rise. A wireless transceiver (TRX) operating in the 400 MHz band is often the preferred choice due to its lower tissue attenuation compared to higher frequency bands. The recently reported transmitters are devoted to achieving higher data rates and lower power consumption through edge-combining technology [1, 2, 4]. However, the use of off-chip matching presents challenges for implantable applications that have stringent volume constraints. Additionally, the lack of receiver and channel selection capabilities limits the suitability of these transmitters for multi-node networking applications. Other transceivers, while compliant with the IEEE 802.15.6 standard for body area networks, suffer from low data rates and poor energy efficiency, as reported in [3, 5]. Thus, a fully integrated transceiver with high data-rate is expected.

articleTitle: A 185-μW, ±2.5-ppm -40°C-80°C Analog TCXO With A Differential-Pair-Based Polynomial Temperature Compensation Technique
abstract: Crystal oscillators (XO) are widely used in electronic systems, providing low-jitter and temperature-stable reference clock signals. The inherent frequency accuracy of XO is good of ± 10ppm within a range of $-40 \sim 80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. However, to have a better accuracy of $\lt \pm 5 \mathrm{ppm}$ for certain applications with harsh operating conditions (e.g. GPS and aerospace), a low-power temperature-compensated XO (TCXO) is desired.

articleTitle: A 5.76 Gb/s 79.7 pJ/b 128×32 Massive Deep-Learning Uplink MIMO Detector in 28nm CMOS Technology
abstract: This work presents the first fabricated massive deep-learning (DL) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector for a $128 \times 32$ antenna configuration and 4 to 256QAM modulations, offering near-optimal detection across diverse channel conditions. Our design employs the fully parallel initialization procedure followed by the fully unfolded DL operations, enhancing the data rate by 13 times compared to the baseline design. We also propose a novel approximate projection to relax the processing cost per layer and a gradient reusing to eliminate all the matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) in the last few layers, saving the overall detector complexity by 38%. Targeting the 256QAM system, our prototype in a 28 nm CMOS process offers a throughput of $5.76 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ and an energy efficiency of $79.7 \mathrm{pJ} / \mathrm{b}$.

articleTitle: A 639.38GOPS Hybrid-Domain Logic-Compatible Multi-Level Embedded Flash Computing-in-Memory Macro with Spike-Edge Computation
abstract: Computing in Memory (CIM) has emerged as a promising research field, significantly reducing power consumption and latency associated with massive data movement and multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations in edge Al devices. For battery-constrained edge devices, non-volatile memories (NVMs) are ideal due to their ability to retain neural network parameters even when powered down, ensuring rapid response time upon device wake-up. Recent studies [2, 3] have integrated NVM into CIM architectures using STT-MRAM and RRAM, achieving high throughput and energy efficiency. Nevertheless, NVMs necessitate specialized fabrication technologies and additional manufacturing steps, which increase process complexity and costs (Fig. 1 (top-left)). As NVM processes advance, these technologies become increasingly challenging to access due to the escalating costs.

articleTitle: A –51dBc-Reference-Spur and 66fsrms-Jitter D-Band PLL with Complementary Power-Gating Injection-Locked Frequency-Multiplier-Based Phase Detector
abstract: Sub-THz frequencies in the W and D bands have received significant attention, and the scope of their application has been extended to cellular communications, radar, and imaging. For these applications, PLL design is especially important to provide precise clock signals at high frequencies above 100 GHz. Cascaded PLLs using a chain of frequency multipliers (FMs) [1–3] are still popular, but they are inefficient in terms of power and silicon area. Single-stage direct PLLs are better suited, but conventional architectures are limited in achieving low jitter due to their inherently high in-band phase noise (PN) [4]. Using a subsampling PD (SSPD) with a high phase-error ($\phi_{\text {ERR }}$)-detection gain, $K_{\text {PD }}$, SSPLLs can reduce the in-band PN. However, this merit is not valid in the sub-THz band where the value of KPD is reduced significantly by the output pole of the SSPD. To ensure a high $K_{P D}$ at such high frequencies, the power-gating injection-locked FM-based PD (PG-ILFM PD) was presented in [5] (top of Fig. 1). With a strong power-gating injection-locking of the replica VCO (RVCO) by the reference clock ($S_{\text {REF }}$), an ultra-low-jitter, high-frequency reference signal, i.e., Silfm, can be generated, and it can be used to detect the $\phi$ ERR of the output of the main VCO (MVCO), i.e., Sout, much more frequently. Based on this mechanism, the PGILFM PD can secure a high $K_{\text {PD }}$, so the D-band PLL in [5] succeeded in achieving a low RMS jitter. However, the PG-ILFM PD has fundamental problems that are caused by its operation, in which the RVCO oscillates only during a half $T_{\text {REF }}$, causing a binary frequency-shift-keying (BFSK) modulation of the frequency of the MVCO (fout). Due to this problem, the PLL in [5] had a high reference spur, i.e., 42dBc. This half-period operation of the PG-ILFM PD also limited the increase of KPD, preventing the further reduction of the RMS jitter.

articleTitle: EnTADRL: Deep Reinforcement Learning System-on-Chip for End-to-End Training Acceleration
abstract: For sequential decision-making problems such as gaming agents and autonomous driving, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) achieves human-level performance by training agents through interactions with the environment [1]. In detail, an agent represented in a deep neural network (DNN) provides action to the environment and the environment offers rewards and states to the agent according to action. By repeating this process, agents are trained to maximize rewards and demonstrate appropriate actions based on the environment. In real-world, environments are dynamic because of new users, new risks and changeable elements, which means the trained agent may fail to demonstrate appropriate actions. Therefore, continuous and efficient DRL training accelerator is necessary for real-world applications.

articleTitle: A 66.6 FPS High Quality Gaussian Splats Rendering FPGA Processor with Reconfigurable Computation Architecture
abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has been a novel solution in rendering 3D scene geometry. Unlike prior works, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), 3DGS can represent scenes using anisotropic covariance parameters as in Fig. 1 [1], enabling high quality rendering in both transparent and reflective scenes with reduced training data [2]. Key stages of rendering process is as follows:1) Frustum Culling - removing gaussians out of view bounds, 2) $2 D$ Feature Computation - computing image parameters from 3D scene parameters, 3) Sorting - aligning gaussians by depth order, 4) Volume Rendering (VR) - accumulating weighted sum of sorted Gaussians to obtain pixel colors.

articleTitle: A 0.28V 80.9μW Transformer-Based DCO with 80kHz 1/f3 corner and 192.6dBc/Hz FoM
abstract: The power constraint of Internet of Things (IoT) nodes causes design challenges for the local oscillator of the transceiver, while the sub-0.5 V and sub- 0.1 mW oscillator design is becoming a trend [1–7]. The ultra-low-voltage (ULV), ultra-low-power (ULP) design of LC oscillators that provide a pure oscillation signal faces difficulty in start-up and amplitude [1].

articleTitle: Development and Applications of a Memory-Traffic-Efficient Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: Built upon circuit insight, HarDNet is introduced as an innovative and efficient convolutional neural network architecture aimed at minimizing DRAM access. This design approach leverages the faster speed and lower energy consumption of arithmetic operations compared to DRAM, resulting in significant improvements in accuracy, speed, and energy efficiency. HarDNet’s optimized architecture makes it well-suited for diverse applications including object detection, semantic segmentation, and medical image analysis. As an open-source initiative, HarD-Net is accessible for global use and adaptation. Its impact spans various domains and regions, from autonomous driving and industrial automation to vehicle safety, environmental monitoring, colonoscopy polyp segmentation, and MRI imaging. Drawing from deployment insights, this presentation outlines challenges and opportunities in circuit and system design to enable robust and cost-effective deep learning solutions. Additionally, it includes case studies of hardware implementations of HarDNet.

articleTitle: A Fully-Connected Time-Modulated Phased-Array Transmitter Featuring Physical Security Directional Link and Multi-Beam PAPR Reduction
abstract: Phased-array techniques have been widely used in wireless and satellite communications. To maximize the communication capacity, multi-beam phased-array architectures have drawn more attention in recent years, which enable simultaneous communication with multiple independent users at different locations [1–2]. A conventional fully-connected topology of the 4-element 4-beam phased-array transmitter (TX) is shown in Fig. 1. The fully-connected phased arrays faces two challenges. First, for each beam of the multi-beam system, the same modulated signal is fed to all the TX elements, transmitting the same information to all directions with different power levels. This information can be demodulated with a sensitive enough eavesdropper receiver (RX). This may lead to the risk of information leakage. Second, one of the key components for a communication TX front-end (FE) is a power amplifier (PA) with relatively high output power and enhanced power-added efficiency (PAE) at both saturated output power (Psat) and power back-off (PBO) levels. The peak-to-average ratio (PAPR) of a modulated signal of $16-Q A M$ is approximately 5.6 dB. For a multi-beam system, when multi-beams operate at the same time, the PA faces an increased PAPR, 8.6dB for 2-beam and 14.6 for 8-beam for example, therefore further deep PBO levels are required, which reduces the overall efficiency and output power of the whole system.

articleTitle: A 24V-to-1.8V Low Input Current Ripple SC Hybrid Converter with Conducted EMI Noise Suppression Mechanism for Automobile Application
abstract: The single-stage 24 V -to- 1 V buck converter can effectively reduce the size of the power module, but its excessive input current ripple will aggravate conducted electromagnetic interference (EMI) noise [1] –[5]. To meet the CISPR 25 standard, large-capacity EMI filters consisting of one inductor and two capacitors are often used, but this takes up a larger printed circuit board (PCB), thereby reducing power density. Double step-down (DSD) converters [1] are suitable for low conversion ratios ($\mathrm{CR}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}} / \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{IN}}$), but suffer from large input current ripple $\left(\Delta I_{\mathbb{I N}}\right)$, equal to $\Delta \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{L} 1}$ during $\Phi_{1}$ (upper right of Fig. 1). I IN ripple will increase at heavy loads, exacerbating conducted EMI noise. Although the inductor L is magnetized and I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">L</inf> is evenly divided into three paths during $\Phi 1$, one of which is powered by $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{IN}}$ in the DPSC converter [3] and I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">L</inf> is almost equal to lo when CR is 1/24 (middle left). A significant increase in $\Delta l \mathrm{ln}$ at heavy loads will also increase EMI noise effects. In the upper right of Fig. 1, [3] can effectively reduce the voltage variation on each switching node, but the significant voltage variation difference between opposite nodes makes it difficult to cancel the EMI noise.

articleTitle: A 4-nm 9.6-Gb/s/pin LPDDR5X PHY With Adaptive Driver Strength Control and Fast Periodic Training for Full DVFS DRAM
abstract: Increasing amount of data processed by mobile devices and automotive systems has accelerated the rapid growth of mobile DRAM bandwidth. Meanwhile, minimizing a power budget to achieve longer battery life is a critical challenge. A WCK clocking scheme and a low voltage-swing terminated logic (LVSTL) driver are adopted in LPDDR5/5X interfaces to meet these requirements with the strictly limited power budget [1–3]. For further power reduction in a system level, a scenario-based dynamic voltage and frequency scaling core (DVFSC) is also employed to minimize the DRAM power consumption by switching the DRAM supply voltage from VDD2H (1.05V) to VDD2L (0.9V) at low data rates [1].

articleTitle: A 75.6Gb/S 22-Bit Floating-Point Reconfigurable DSP Accelerator Embedding 2048×256-Point Complex FFT and 26K-Point 1-D Signal Processing
abstract: 77 GHz band millimeter-wave radar is a highly popular research topic with broad application prospects in areas such as autonomous driving. However, as shown in Fig. 1, with the advancement of radar technology, the performance requirements for dedicated DSP accelerators [1–4] have also risen, presenting the following new challenges:1) Diversified computational tasks based on dynamically changing data flows, necessitating efficient execution of different workloads, 2) Demands for increased resolution and range for detection, requiring large-scale processing elements (PEs) with real-time low latency, 3) Desire for better data accuracy and multi-channel inputs, leading to high data throughput.

articleTitle: A 16-30Gb/s 1.03pJ/b Referenceless Baud-Rate CDR with Integrated Pattern Decoding Technique for Fast Frequency Acquisition
abstract: Referenceless clock and data recovery (CDR) circuits operate across a range of data rates without an external reference clock. To operate over a range of data rates, several frequency acquisition techniques have been proposed [1–5]. Oversampling CDRs utilize additional clock phases with more than one sample per unit interval (UI), achieving robust frequency acquisition [1–3]. However, due to the additional clock phases, the oversampling CDRs have difficulty in multi-phase clock generation and large power consumption of clock buffers. Compared with the oversampling CDRs, a baud-rate CDR requires one clock phase per UI, reducing the problem from the multi-phase clocking with a reduced number of clock phases. However, previous referenceless CDRs with the baud-rate sampling have increased frequency acquisition time compared to the oversampling CDRs [4–5]. In this work, a referenceless baud-rate CDR with an integrated pattern decoding technique is proposed. While reducing the number of clock phases, the proposed CDR achieves reduced frequency acquisition time by applying weights to divided pattern groups in the integrated pattern decoding logic.

articleTitle: LPNA: A 2.75 ms Low-Latency and 0.40 uJ/point Energy-Efficient LiDAR Point-Cloud Neural Network Accelerator with Cylindrical Bin Partitioning
abstract: As the interest in 3D perception for outdoor applications grows, 3D Point-cloud Neural Network (PNN) with LiDAR has been actively developed [1]. Due to the unstructured and unordered properties of point-cloud, prior PNNs applied additional preprocessing, e.g., voxelization, 3D projection, even though such methods lose point data. To achieve high performance in 3D segmentation, recent PNNs directly use point-cloud data as input and learn accurate point-wise features [2]. However, such a network requires a serial process of special functions, e.g., k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) search and shared multi-layer perception (MLP), due to the properties of point-cloud. The serial process of kNN search and shared MLP causes long processing latency. Also, a large amount of external memory access (EMA) is inevitable in decoder layers for interpolation. Thus, PNN solely takes $\sim 335 \mathrm{~ms}$ on a high-end CPU+ GPU system (Fig.1).

articleTitle: A Single-Ended Offset-Compensating Bit-Line Sense-Amplifier with Ground Precharge and Charge Transfer Pre sensing for Sub-1V DRAM
abstract: Over the past two decades the DRAM products have consistently decreased the supply voltage for advances in the energy required to access and store data in memory cells. In addition, as the DRAM technology scales, the capacitance (Cs) to store data polarity gradually decreases and the discrepancy of the transistor’s key parameters, such as threshold voltage, increases. Therefore, bit-line sense amplifier (BLSA) with high sensitivity is essential. Traditionally, the BLSAs rely on cross-coupled latch with $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{cca}} / 2$ precharge topology due to their balanced characteristic between data “ 1 “ and “ 0 “, and many studies have been investigated to improve its sensitivity. Fig. 1(a) shows the prior offset compensation sense amplifier (OCSA). To mitigate the BLSA’s offset, $\phi_{1}$ is tuned on before the enabling word line (WL) and at the end of $\phi_{1}$ phase the offset of BLSAs is minimized [1], [4]. The OCSA offers a sensitivity solution and benefit from fast settling speed using positive feedback during the offset compensation phase. However, with the low supply applications, high-speed operation and device reliability are limited due to the $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{cca}} / 2$ precharge topology.

articleTitle: A Multi-Node Body-Channel-Communication System Using Adaptive Gain Control with ExG Readout ICs for Moving VR Users
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and extended reality (XR) technologies have been utilized to enhance realism in gaming, exercise, military training, and other applications beyond spatial constraints. Besides visual advancements, it is crucial to monitor the movements of each arm and leg in real time for practical human motion analysis. However, connecting the modules on each limb using wires limits the user’s movement and causes user inconvenience, and wireless connection suffers from high power consumption, which hinders the development of wearable and long-lasting solutions. By employing body-channel communication (BCC), we can achieve user’s free and comfortable movement, high energy efficiency, and low cost, all at the same time. It also enables real-time, wireless acquisition of electromyography (EMG) signals from all the arms and legs, as well as electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, without the constraints of wires.

articleTitle: A 1.96Vpp Input-Range 3rd-order Noise-Shaping Pipelined-SAR ADC with Self-Boosted Impedance and Active Charge Sharing for Biosignal Acquisition
abstract: Wearable healthcare devices require front ends with high input impedance (Ziv), low power and high resolution (uV-level) with area efficiency in the presence of large artifacts and DC offset. The conventional architecture of instrument amplifier (IA)+ADC has low dynamic range (DR), suffering from artifacts which easily cause IAs saturation [1], [2]. In contrast, the direct-conversion ADC front end is promising due to its high DR with lower power. The continuous-time DSM (CTDSM) is advantageous in $\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{IN}}$ and area [3], but suffers from 1/f noise and limited input range. CTDSMs with the chopping technique [4]–[6] mitigate 1/f noise at the cost of reduced Zin (Fig. 1 (a)). SAR/Noise shaping (NS)-SAR ADCs [7–9] have intrinsic large input range, hence being tolerable to artifacts and offset (Fig.1(b)). However, due to the large sampling capacitor limited by kT/C noise, $\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{IN}}$ and area efficiency of the NS-SAR ADC are low, which hinders its adoption in biosignal acquisition. Moreover, the state-of-the-art (SOTA) direct-conversion ADC require a separate accuracy-limited Zin booster for high Zin and a high over-sampling rate (OSR) for high resolution, which degrades power and hardware efficiency.

articleTitle: A 16-bit SAR ADC with Capacitor Dielectric Relaxation Effect Canceler in a 22-nm Microcontroller for Multi-Input Channel Applications
abstract: Because general-purpose microcontrollers (MCUs) handle input signals from wide variety of sensors, ADCs must support sampling frequencies of a few MHz, 16-bit resolution, and single-ended and common-free differential inputs. The ADC shown in Fig. 1(a) multiplexes input channels (CHs) to support low-cost multi-input systems, and uses oversampling techniques and digital filters to suppress noise from the CPU, RAM, ROM, and I/O. In addition, motor control applications require that the sampling skew of each CH must be suppressed. Therefore, as shown in Fig. 1(d), the input CH is switched by a multiplexer for each A/D conversion, and the output of the ADC is distributed to a digital filter dedicated to each CH by a demultiplexer. However, in such a system, the SNDR is degraded by interference with the residual signal from the previous channel due to the capacitor dielectric relaxation effect [1] [2]. The capacitor dielectric relaxation effect is a frequency-dependent change in capacitance that can be represented by a combination of several RC models. The problem is that the dielectric relaxation effect exists down to the low frequency bands in Fig. 1(b), so the speed of the ADC must be reduced, and this effect is especially significant in high accuracy ADCs.

articleTitle: SRAM Physically Unclonable Function Extracting Static Entropy from Every Bitcell Transistor for 6 bit/bitcell and Data Fingerprinting Capability for Provenance Assurance
abstract: An SRAM physically unclonable function (PUF) uniquely extracting static entropy from every transistor of an unmodified $6 T$ bitcell for 6 bit/bitcell is presented. The proposed multi-bit SRAM PUF achieves state-of-the-art 296% PUF-to-SRAM capacity, while not requiring any ECC to retain the same energy and area efficiency at system level. In addition to PUF operation, its unique data-dependent static entropy extraction enables data fingerprinting capability. The latter represents an additional layer of security providing stored data (physical) provenance assurance, and user authentication in real time or in retrospect. After one-time calibration, the proposed current-mode periphery extracts PUF bitstreams with native cryptography-grade quality while suppressing any post-processing circuitry, retaining its competitive $134 \mathrm{~F}^{2} /$ bit area efficiency at system level.

articleTitle: A 10kHz-BW 24.9μW 90.1dB SNDR Noise-Shaping SAR ADC With Complementary Parametric Amplifiers
abstract: Noise shaping successive-approximation-register (NS SAR) analog-to-digital converters (ADC) have shown excellent power efficiency and received popularity in power-constrained designs with high precision requirements, such as loT sensor instrumentation and brain machine interface. Active or passive quantization error amplification is usually required to realize filter shaping [1–2]. The noise and power consumption of the residual amplifier (RA) become one of the important factors limiting the overall ADC performance. Many quantization error amplifiers already exist for design trade-off between power, area and noise, such as duty cycle amplifiers (DCA) [2], gmR amplifiers [3–4], dynamic amplifiers, floating inverter amplifiers (FIA) [5], capacitors stacking [6], etc. In this work, we propose to use passive differential complementary parametric amplifier with kT/C noise dominance and near-zero power consumption to form RA. To demonstrate this technique, an 8 -bit ADC is designed. Fabricated in a typical 180 nm CMOS process, the prototype ADC achieves 90.1 dB SNDR over a 10 kHz bandwidth with an OSR of 12.5 and consumes $24.9 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ from a 1.8 V supply voltage, resulting in a SNDR based Schreier FoM of 176.2dB.

articleTitle: A 64-channel SPAD-based LiDAR sensor with Compact Coincidence Detection Circuit and Inter-frame Correlation-based Nonlinear Partial Histogram Builder
abstract: The SPAD-based Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensor [1–3] has found widespread applications across various fields, including consumer electronics, surveillance, and autonomous driving [4]. Leveraging collimated laser beams, line sensors are particularly suitable for outdoor applications due to its inherently higher optical signal-to-background ratio (SBR). However, detection range can still be limited in the presence of high background noise and constrained laser power budget. Macro pixels that incorporate coincidence detection circuits (CDC) aid in filtering events generated by background light through the utilization of temporal and spatial correlations among the detected signal photons [4]. Nonetheless, concurrently achieving compact coincidence detection, adjustable coincidence threshold settings, and PVT-insensitive correlation window generation remains a challenge using current methods [2, 4, 5]. To achieve high spatial resolution, scanning technique can be employed, albeit at the cost of potentially reducing the frame rate. In order to maintain an acceptable frame rate, the number of accumulated laser shots within each frame should be limited. In this scenario, the use of the traditional linear histogram builder method can decrease the SBR and consequently impact the detection range. To address these challenges, a 64-channel SPAD-based scanning LiDAR sensor is proposed. The main contributions of this work include: (1) Proposal of a compact and precise CDC for filtering out uncorrelated events. (2) Introduction of an inter-frame correlation-based nonlinear histogram builder and frame adjustment strategy intended to resolve the tradeoff between SBR and frame rate.

articleTitle: A Wide Current Range and Fast Transient Flipped Voltage Follower Based Low Dropout Regulator
abstract: Flipped voltage follower (FVF) based low dropout regulators (LDOs) have been developed rapidly in recent years due to their low circuit complexity, fast transient response and high power supply rejection (PSR). The FVF can be used to replicate the reference voltage ($\mathrm{V}_{\text {REF }}$) as the output voltage (Vout) of the LDO and then conduct feedback regulation [1], or implement a fully integrated fast response loop [2]. The conventional FVF loop encounters stability challenges under heavy load conditions when employing dominant pole compensation with a large output capacitance. The load-dependent dominant pole ($\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{o}}$) at the output of the LDO causes an increase in unity-gain frequency (UGF) when the load current increases, and thus the maximum load current is limited by the poles at the output of the gain stage and at the gate of the power transistor.

articleTitle: A 28nm 76.25TOPS/W RRAM/SRAM-Collaborative CIM Fine-Tuning Accelerator with RRAM-Endurance/Latency-Aware Weight Allocation for CNN and Transformer
abstract: Fine-tuning stands out as an emerging trend in recent machine learning systems, offering significant utility across domains from transfer learning, large language models to privacy-sensitive tasks on edge [1]. In the context of fine-tuning, it is an efficient practice to preserve most parameters of the pre-trained feature extraction layers and re-train the weights associated with the fully connected (FC) layers based on a new yet limited dataset. Embedded non-volatile memory (NVM) based CIMs, such as RRAM, and SoCs feature high area and energy efficiency [2]. Also, the multi-chip RRAM accelerator has realized DNN computing without off-chip memory [3]. However, incorporating fine-tuning or training into RRAM-based hardware poses the following challenges (Fig. 1): 1) The frequent weight updating of fine-tuning is limited by NVM endurance, the finite number of times an NVM cell can be written before it wears out; 2) The weight updating process is subject to notable deceleration due to the write and verification latency of RRAM; 3) Higher precision and more storage are desired to represent weight gradients (WG) in finetuning than inference-only accelerators. Previous RRAM-based neural network accelerators that accommodate fine-tuning [5] often include a dedicated SRAM module to replicate higher bit-width weights, resulting in a large on-chip area and power consumption. RRAM modules are not involved in the training or fine-tuning process.

articleTitle: A 4-Phase Integrated Voltage Regulator with In-Package Inductors Achieving 89.0% Peak Efficiency and 65% Droop Improvement for 6A/2ns Transient
abstract: With the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), computing processors and GPUs have dramatically increased their current consumption. Significant power ($I^{2} R$) losses and heat can be generated on the routing path between the voltage regulators (VRs) and the processors, as shown in Fig. 1. To address this issue, VRs are required to possess high current density and high efficiency, ensuring they can be placed closest to the processors and do not generate excessive heat. The inductors in VRs present the greatest challenge in minimizing the size due to their low power density and difficulty of integration. Fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs) in [1], [2] employed high-performance in-package air-core/magnetic inductors to achieve high current density and efficiency. However, they require expensive and exclusive inductor fabrication processes. In [3], a switched-capacitor voltage regulator (SCVR) was adopted to avoid inductors and establish a compact volume. However, deeptrenched capacitors were required and slow transient responses were observed. Additionally, multiphase FIVRs utilizing bond-wires as inductors [4], [5] have been explored, but their maximum output current (lout) is limited, and bond-wires are incompatible with flip-chip packages. Moreover, VRs must have fast transient response to stabilize output voltage during extreme load fluctuations in processors while current transient-enhancement techniques cannot cope with various transient conditions and may still experience large undershoot.

articleTitle: A nMOS-Only Pulse-Width Modulation CMOS Imager with Body Effect Mitigation Using Differential Comparison Technique
abstract: The emergence of 3D-stacking in semiconductor technology has revolutionized CIS chip design, offering enhanced performance and efficiency in a smaller form factor. Pulse-width modulation (PWM) pixels are favored for stacking due to the time-domain output with immunity to interconnection impedance and downstream noise. Recent research simplified comparator designs, enabling the integration of all pixel devices into stacked chips. However, in the latest 3-layer wafer stacking processes, the intermediate layer can only accommodate NMOS design, posing a challenge for achieving an NMOS-only PWM pixel circuit. Current research on PWM pixel circuits mainly focuses on two types of architecture. The first type, proposed in [1–2], employs a common source as the in-pixel comparator, enabling a high-gain output at low voltages, however, requiring the use of PMOS. Moreover, the voltage gain, which depends on the input signal, may affect the circuit linearity. The second type, proposed in [3–5], uses NMOS as a switch, benefiting from using only NMOS components. However, the conductivity of an NMOS switch also depends on the threshold voltage and body effect, leading to signal-dependent variations which impact the overall linearity. Thus, mitigating the body effect is crucial for achieving high linearity. In this work, in-pixel voltage-to-time conversion is achieved by using only three NMOS devices, while the influence of body effect on the linear response is addressed through the proposed differential comparison technique.

articleTitle: 35-60GHz Switchless IF Bi-Directional Amplifier Using 65nm CMOS for 300GHz-Band Transceivers
abstract: The escalating demand for enhanced wireless communication performance has spurred significant interest in sub-THz frequency bands, notably the J-band (220-325GHz). This band stands out due to an established IEEE standard (802.15.3d), which supports channel widths of up to 69GHz. However, designing amplifiers for such high frequencies requires innovative approaches, such as adopting mixer-last or mixer-first topologies, where the IF amplifiers provide the necessary amplification. Additionally, achieving satisfactory power levels involves the integration of phased-array structures, underscoring the importance of area minimization [1], [2]. This paper delves into the methodologies associated with device de-embedding and modeling. It further details the design of a bi-directional IF amplifier, realized in a 65nm CMOS process with a core area of 1.45x0.3mm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. The amplifier’s measured performance achieves a 14dB gain across a 25GHz bandwidth (35-60GHz) in both transmission directions, an 8.4dB noise figure (NF) for the LNA, and a 7dBm OIP3 for the PA. It also supports 125Gb/s communication employing 32QAM modulation, which significantly advances sub-THz wireless communication.

articleTitle: KDA: Kyber and Dilithium Accelerator for CRYSTALS Suite of Post-Quantum Cryptography in Hybrid Multipath Delay Commutator Pipelined Architecture
abstract: The emergence and rise of quantum computers have shattered people’s trust in traditional cryptographic systems. They execute algorithms such as Shor, Grover, and quantum Fourier transform, which can break classical public-key cryptography and digital signatures within a limited time. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has approved the draft FIPS-203 and FIPS204 post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards based on module lattices. These are the twin cryptos of the CRYSTALS suite, Kyber and Dilithium, which serve as key-encapsulation mechanisms (KEM) and digital signatures (DS), respectively. The migration to PQC requires the cooperation of both. In this paper, we propose a hybrid multipath delay commutator pipelined architecture (HMDC) for a fused hardware accelerator for Kyber and Dilithium. It utilizes switchable parallel and MDC serial pipeline architectures to achieve fast number-theoretic transform (NTT) operations. Multipliers are reused in vertical or horizontal modes through Karatsuba and Barrett methods, compatible with different algorithm parameters. Efficient cascaded Keccak structures and multi-mode cryptographic processing address various operations. This accelerator supports both Kyber and Dilithium algorithms, achieving the highest frequency and speed among similar designs due to the HMDC architecture.

articleTitle: A Tiny 3.15–43.4-GHz 3.6-mW Divide-by-8 Ring-Based Injection-Locked Frequency Divider Using Multiphase Waveform Gating Technique
abstract: To support high-speed complex modulation in the 5 G mm-wave bands (i.e. $24.25-43.5 \mathrm{GHz}$), mm-wave PLLs should provide low rms jitter while consuming low power [1]. To ensure their robust operation across such a wide frequency span, a key issue is to guarantee the proper functionality of the divider chain to correctly down-convert the oscillator’s mm-wave signal to the neighborhood frequency of the reference clock. As the first (i.e. mm-wave) divider stage, a current-mode logic (CML) divider or an injection-locked frequency divider (ILFD) is usually chosen but they suffer from high dc power or a limited locking range (LR), respectively [2–3]. Despite an acceptable LR [4–7], the division ratio is usually less than 5. To avoid the additional power/area penalty of subsequent divider stages, a high division-ratio ILFD (e.g. $\div 8$) with a wide LR is desired. Figure 1(a) presents a conventional high-division-ratio ILFD based on an N stage delay cell, but the injecting signal is only fed to the tail transistor of the first-stage delay cell, thereby offering only a limited LR.

articleTitle: A 12b 3 GS/s Passive T/H Assisted Time-Interleaved Pipelined SAR ADC with Metastability Reduction Technique and Dynamic-Bias RA
abstract: Time-interleaved (TI) ADCs present an ingenious solution to accelerate conversion rates with minimal power penalty. However, mismatches from interleaved channels, such as gain, offset, timing mismatches, are main challenges. In particular, timing mismatches, including skew and bandwidth mismatches, are nontrivial to tackle when aiming for input-independent calibration. Analog skew detection techniques [1], randomization of the interleaved channels [2–3], power-hungry full-speed track-and-hold (T/H) [3] and dither injection in the input buffer [4–5] have been developed to tackle this issue. This work utilizes a power-efficient passive T/H with less overhead. Another fundamental limitation of high-speed SAR ADCs is high CER due to comparator metastability. Prior works [6–7] processes metastability detection with the accurate information of comparator decision time (CDT) at the cost of circuit complexity. The proposed metastability reduction technique can remarkably reduce CER with a little additional delay. Operating at $3 \mathrm{GS} / \mathrm{s}$, this prototype ADC achieves a FoMw of $15.5 \mathrm{fJ} /$ conversion-step.

articleTitle: A W-Band Scalable 1 × 4 Phased-Array Transmitter Front-End with >15/17 dBm OP1dB/Psat in SiGe BiCMOS
abstract: Due to the relatively low atmospheric attenuation, about $0.4 \mathrm{~dB} / \mathrm{km}$ at sea level, W-band frequencies in general and 94 GHz in particular have been widely used in various phased-array systems, including communication [1], radar [2] and imaging. Some highly integrated phased-arrays [1–4] and the associated scalability techniques [1], [5] have been implemented at 94 GHz. However, most of the silicon-based phased-arrays at W -band have low output-referred 1-dB compression point $\left(\mathrm{OP}_{1 \mathrm{~dB}}\right)$ and saturated output power $\left(\mathrm{P}_{\text {sat }}\right)$. It is widely known that the array scale needs to be doubled to obtain the same effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) when the output power per channel drops by 6 dB. This will result in larger power consumption and chip area.

articleTitle: A 28nm 166.9 TOPS/W x Mb/mm2 DRAM-Free QLC Compute-in-ROM Macro Supporting High Task-Level Inference Energy Efficiency for Tiny AI Edge Devices
abstract: Compute-in-Memory (CiM) is recognized as a promising approach to mitigating the high communication costs due to the “memory wall” bottleneck in the traditional von Neumann architecture. Given the advancements in the Internet-of-Things (IOT) and artificial intelligence (AI), where neural network (NN) models are continually increasing in size and complexity, large storage CiM holds promise for accelerating deep NN (DNNs) on resource-constrained edge devices, enabling efficient processing with minimal or no weights loading from off-chip memory. However, as illustrated in Fig. 1, there are two primary challenges that hinder existing CiM solutions [2–6] for edge Al applications: (1) the high cost of off-chip data movement due to low on-chip CiM macro density, and (2) the trade-off between CiM output A/D conversion (ADC) precision, energy, and throughput in multi-bit multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations.

articleTitle: A 2.8-to-7.2GT/s DDR5 Registering Clock Driver IC with Parallel-Data Timing and Pin-to-Pin Skew Calibration for a Dual In-Line Memory Module
abstract: The big-data platforms such as data centers and servers require high-speed, high-density, and low-energy dual in-line memory module (DIMM) including an array of DRAMs mounted on a small board in Fig. 1. Each DRAM is working based on the double data rate (DDR) memory interface to accomplish $2 x$ speed compared to its counterpart, single data rate (SDR). However, the rapidly growing CPU speed has needed more the number of DRAMs on the DIMM board, leading to a necessity of a registering clock driver (RCD) IC [1]. It plays a critical role in connecting the CPU and 40EA DRAMs through a time-interleaved DRAM operation by segmenting the the DIMM board to 2-channels (A, B) and 2-groups (A, B). In other words, the RCD IC should enhance the timing synchronization among memory modules by refining the command-address ($\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{CA}}$) data and the chip-selection ($\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{cs}}$) data along with the differential clock ($\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{ck}}$) from the CPU. Additionally, it significantly contributes to the system stability improvement by ensuring the consistent signal transmissions, but the bandwidth evolution to $4^{\text {th }}$-generation ($7.2 \mathrm{GT} / \mathrm{s}$) causes formidable challenges in processing 7-bit Dca, 2-bit Dcs and 1-differential Dck and transmitting refined 14bit Qca, 2-bit Qcs and 2-differential Qck with the minimal pin-to-pin skew ($\lt \pm 2.5 \mathrm{ps}$) to 40EA DRAMs. To overcome these issues, we present a $7.2 \mathrm{GT} / \mathrm{s}$ RCD IC for the DDR5 DIMM. The proposed timing calibration strategy based on a PVT-insensitive digital-to-time converter (DTC) and a phase-interpolator (PI)-offset control ensures stable data processing of $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{CA}}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{cs}}$. The PI-imbedded PLL mitigates the timing slack through jitter-filtering of Dck input (4.72 to $0.20 \mathrm{ps} r \mathrm{~ms}$ at 3.6 GHz). Additionally, the auxiliary-DAC (A-DAC)-based current-mode PI (CMPI) compensates for phase and amplitude distortions of the conventional CMPI, yielding $\mathbb{N L}_{p-p}$ of ${\lt}1.06 \mathrm{LSB}$ at 3.6GHz. Finally, the proposed skew calibration strategy allocating an additional PI-offset control per group and a DTC per pin allows the skew to be $\lt \pm 1.6$ ps.

articleTitle: A reduced complexity MLSD-based adaptive Duo-PAM4 detector in 28-nm CMOS for 56-Gb/s wireline receiver
abstract: The bandwidth demand for long-reach (LR) PAM4 wireline transceivers is growing rapidly. When the channel insertion loss (IL) is greater than 20 dB, the increased inter-symbol interference (ISI) associated with a high bit rate can greatly increase the bit error rate (BER) [1]. The duobinary four-level pulse amplitude modulation (Duo-PAM4) signal has a lower bandwidth compared to the PAM4 signal and is studied in high IL and high-speed serial links [2–4]. However, its more complex structure makes it more demanding in terms of equalization capability. The conventional decision feedback equalization (DFE) approach is difficult to implement in high-speed wireline transceivers due to its short feedback loop and propagation of errors [5]. In this paper, we propose a reduced branch maximum likelihood sequence detector (RB-MLSD) for Duo-PAM4 for high-speed ADC-DSP transceivers, which accomplishes both detection and decoding simultaneously and avoids the disadvantages of timing constraints and error propagation of the conventional DFE and slicer scheme. Meanwhile, we propose an improved zero-forced algorithm for Duo-PAM4 (ZF-Duo-PAM4), which reduces the problem of long convergence time of the FFE tap coefficient when the conventional ZF algorithm is applied to Duo-PAM4.

articleTitle: DPe-CIM: A 4T1C Dual-Port eDRAM Compute-in-Memory for Simultaneous Computing and Refresh with Adaptive Refresh and Data Conversion Reduction Scheme
abstract: Recently, eDRAM-based computing-in-memory operating in analog domain (ACIM) has been proposed to enhance area and energy efficiency of AI computations [1–5]. However, conventional ACIMs have three challenges. First, previous structures [1–3] have primarily focused on computing area or energy efficiency without considering refresh overhead. This may not be a problem in small DNN models. However, as shown in Fig. 1, refresh overhead has become critical with the increase in DNN model size for higher accuracy and the decrease in data retention time (DRT) due to technology scaling. Second, a pre-measured refresh period at the worst corner used in [4, 5] causes unnecessary energy consumption in most PVT corners, as DRT in eDRAM significantly varies depending on the PVT corner. The last challenge is the significant area and energy overhead of data conversion circuits (DAC or ADC) required in ACIMs to ensure DNN accuracy [4–8].

articleTitle: A 5× OSR 1MHz-BW 81dB-SNDR 5th-Order Noise-Shaping SAR ADC with Zero-Optimized 3rd-Order Integrator
abstract: Noise-shaping (NS) SAR ADCs have become very popular architecture for their low-power high-resolution characteristics. However, designing a highly energy-efficient NS SAR with low OSRs is challenging. It requires simple and low-power hardware to achieve high-order optimized noise transfer functions (NTF) that maximally preserves the efficient nature of the SAR. Classic single-loop NS designs typically employ CIFF structure, but the complexity of the NS filter increases drastically with the NTF order [1]. A recent work in [2] reported a $4^{\text {th }}$-order NS having an aggressive NTF utilizing a buffer-assisted CIFF structure with only simple open-loop amps. However, it lacks NTF optimization capability, making it unsuitable for low-OSR designs. In addition, the static power consumption by the buffers degrades the energy efficiency. Another work in [3] presented a low-complexity cascaded EF structure where a $4^{\text {th }}$-order NTF was implemented by nesting two simple $2^{\text {nd }}-$ order filters with comparable hardware overhead to that of $2^{\text {nd }}$-order NTF. Nevertheless, this structure suffers from SQNR fluctuation and relatively low offset tolerance.

articleTitle: A 13.75-14.75-GHz 32.1-fsRMS Jitter -100.6-dBc Reference Spur -261.4-dB FoM Sub-Sampling PLL Using a KPD-Doubled Isolated Sub-Sampling Phase Detector for Reliable Spur-Jitter-Joint Optimization
abstract: With the continuous increase in the communication data rate, low-jitter phase-locked loop (PLL) is increasingly becoming significant for ultra-high-speed wireless or wireline transceivers [1], namely the concurrent realization of low jitter and low spur. The most advanced PLL design has achieved sub-50-fs jitter [2–6], as summarized in Fig.1. The reference sampling PLL (RS-PLL) [2] achieves low jitter and low power due to the removal of input reference clock buffer and its simple architecture. But the clock feedthrough from the reference clock to the tuning voltage of the voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) limits its spur performance, and the direct sampling operation to the reference clock from crystal induces disturbance to other blocks in the system. The sampling PLL (S-PLL) [3, 4] can avoid these issues, and achieves very low clock jitter using a double-edge sampling phase detector (PD); yet, the PLL in [3] requires a complicated and power-hungry retimer to realize a low-jitter high-frequency divider chain, and the mismatch of duty cycle correction (DCC) circuit degrades the spur to >-70 dBc. Multi-reference PLL (MR-PLL) [5] achieves the state-of-the-art low jitter but it consumes huge power due to the adoption of multiple reference clock sources with multiple SPDs; meanwhile, large numbers of switches in its multiple SPDs also cause higher-level feedthrough to VCO, thus limiting spur. Alternatively, the sub-sampling PLL (SS-PLL) with isolation subsampling PD (iSSPD) achieves sub-35-fs jitter and $\lt-90-\mathrm{dBc}$ spur concurrently with a low-power retime-less divider [6]. However, its spur-jitter-joint optimization relies on an ultra-high VCO swing and small-sized iSSPD to suppress the PD’s interference to VCO with a sufficient iSSPD gain (KPD), hence leading to a reliability issue with a relatively high VCO power.

articleTitle: A Passive IoT Bidirectional Tag Demonstrating 95m Downlink through Antenna-Array-Based Power-Data-Fusion Technique
abstract: The future boosting of loT applications is limited by the mW-level power burden of widely deployed wireless communication chips such as WiFi [1] and BLE [2]. As shown in Fig. 1 (top), the standby power leads to significant energy wastage in long-term loT sensors integrated with active radios. The traditional RFID-like devices offer a zero-standby wake-up solution [3], but the NFC suffers from ${\lt}10 \mathrm{~cm}$ short range and far-field RFID requires dedicated high-cost reader hardware. In recent years, battery-free techniques have been explored to support widely-used standards such as WiFi [4] and BLE [5], to realize seamlessly integration with the current infrastructure. Although the uplink channel has been extended to 160 m [6], the effective downlink range is limited to ${\lt}30 \mathrm{~m}$ [4–6] due to the poor sensitivity of power harvester based signal receiver.

articleTitle: A 0.6V Fully-Integrated BLE Transmitter in 65nm CMOS Using a Common-Mode-Ripple-Cancelled Hybrid PLL and a Duty-Cycle-Controlled Class-E/F2 PA Achieving 25% System Efficiency at 0dBm
abstract: Low-cost high-efficiency BLE transmitters (TXs) are highly demanded for short-range wireless connectivity. The system efficiency of previous BLE TXs is mainly limited by PLL and PA performance to satisfy BLE requirements [1]–[3]. In this work, a 0.6 V fully-integrated BLE TX shown in Fig. 1 is proposed to achieve 25% system efficiency at 0 dBm output with following features: (1) a submW RDAC-based hybrid PLL [4] with common-mode (CM) ripple cancellation to reduce reference spur; (2) a switching current-source (SCS) D/VCO with a step-up transformer and a shared bias resistor for differential varactors to improve efficiency and phase noise; (3) a duty-cycle controlled class-E/F<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> digital PA to suppress $3^{\text {rd }}$-harmonic distortion $\left(\mathrm{HD}_{3}\right)$ without degrading PA efficiency; (4) a calibration-free 1-bit $\Delta \Sigma$ high-pass modulation with FIR filtering to overcome the nonlinearity issue of a low-voltage DCO in two-point modulation [5].

articleTitle: A 10.5 Gbps 0.55 pJ/bit PAM-3 Transceiver Using a Self-driven Dual TIA Receiver and Floating Impedance Matching for Parallel On-chip Transmission Lines
abstract: The demand for high-bandwidth and parallel interconnection for memory interfaces is steadily increasing [1]–[5]. The top of Fig. 1 shows three popular structures for the memory interface. Non-return to zero (NRZ) signaling with a termination resistor has the simplest structure. However, NRZ signaling suffers from significant channel loss and power consumption due to the high clock frequency. Pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) has been proposed to extend the data rate by sending multi-bit per unit interval. However, PAM-4 consumes significant static current for intermediate levels and has a poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Thus, complicated equalizing techniques are employed, leading to significant power consumption. However, PAM-3 offers a higher SNR, and removes the reference voltage (VREF) using inverter-based TIA, which makes PAM-3 transceivers more area- and power-efficient than PAM-4. However, the large static current at the Mid-level is still the fundamental limitation of PAM-3. Therefore, this paper proposes the self-driven receiver (SDR) to remove the static current in the PAM-3 transmitter (Tx) by deactivating it. The floating impedance matching (FIM) for the Mid-level reduces the channel reflections at the deactivated Tx. Finally, the dual TIAs in SDR improve signal integrity by separating the top and bottom eyes, and reduce power consumption by employing biased inverters.

articleTitle: A 28-nm 323 TOPS/mm2/b and 2007 TOPS/W/b Ternary Latch Based Sparsity-Aware CIM Macro With Double-Sampling Ternary ADC
abstract: For resource constrained on-device Al environment, system efficiency is the key factor for successful implementation (Fig. 1): area efficiency (TOPS $/ \mathrm{mm}^{2}$) to inference the user demand AI task while maintaining device size to a palm-scale, and power efficiency (TOPS/W) for maximum application usage on limited battery life. To save resources, network precisions are quantized and sparsity exploitable ternary $(-1,0,+1)$ input/weight shows best outcome as hardware demonstration in [1] achieves -82% energy per inference compared to binary ($-1,+1$). For system architecture, analog designs generally have high efficiency, as custom bitcells are compactly integrated and perform multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations in parallel with low energy consumption. However, there are two challenges that degrade the efficiency enhancement. 1) For bitcells, it requires an additional latch for ternary weight and reduces macro area efficiency. 2) In analog compute-in-memory (CIM), increase in number of MAC worsens the energy and signal margin which affects operation’s accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, A-to-D converters (ADCs) occupy 41% of macro area [2] and 72% latency [3], so minimal overhead is crucial for analog CIM system efficiency. In this paper we present highly resource efficient ternary latch based CIM macro 1) The refined single latch ternary input/weight cell enabled by 28 nm ternary-CMOS (T-CMOS) technology. 2) Solutions for analog CIM performance enhancement by energy-efficient and signal margin improved MAC operation with double-sampling ternary ADC.

articleTitle: A 39-Gb/s PAM-3 Transmitter and ADC-Based Receiver Chipset in CMOS Technologies
abstract: Recently, the pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) signaling has been extensively applied in wireline communication. Comparing with the PAM-4 counterpart, the PAM-3 signaling provides another solution to increase the data rate with less SNR degradation and linearity requirement. It is adopted in the recent USB4 2.0 specification with $40-\mathrm{Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ per-lane data rate [1]. This paper presents a $39-\mathrm{Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ PAM3 TXIRX chipset in 40 - and $28-\mathrm{nm}$ CMOS technologies. The TX and RX achieves 2.2- and 4.3-pJ/b energy efficiency, respectively. The RX adopts the ADC-DSP architecture with digital equalization to achieve 1E-8 pre-FEC BER under $27-\mathrm{dB}$ loss channel.

articleTitle: Compact Hybrid Strong SOIPUF Exploiting Secret Key Generation and Dual-Edge Response Extraction for Enhanced Modeling Attack Resistance
abstract: With a huge number of device-specific challenge response pairs (CRPs), strong physical unclonable function (PUF) is a promising technology for low-cost loT device authorization. However, they are typically vulnerable to machine learning (ML) attacks due to the correlation among CRPs. Even though the existing hybrid strong PUFs (weak PUF assisted strong PUF) such as PRNG [1], AESSbox [2] and SPN [3] can ensure a high security through utilizing a huge amount of weak PUFs and extensive nonlinear computations, their complex implementation can result in an extremely large area overhead (e.g., 16.7 $\mathrm{MF}^{2}$ in [1], 23.8 $\mathrm{MF}^{2}$ in [2], and $25 \mathrm{MF}^{2}$ in [3], respectively). By taking advantage of the highly compact property of arbiter-based PUFs and addressing its weakness in ML resilience, this work presents a hybrid strong PUF using symmetrical obfuscated interconnection (SOI) [4], with the secret key generator (SKG) array for challenge obfuscation to combat against both black box and white box ML attacks while requiring an area of only $3.8 \mathrm{MF}^{2}$. Moreover, unlike the conventional arbiter-based PUFs that only employs one single edge as the trigger signal, we further propose the dual-edge (DE) response extraction technique to fully utilize the entropy sources from the SOI block for enhancing both the security and randomness with minimal hardware overhead. We further introduce the meta-stable detection (MD) technique to enhance the PUF reliability. This work can attain a measured ML prediction accuracy of 50.04% with up to 20 M training CRPs and a worse-case bit error rate (BER) of $4 \times 10^{-6}$, while achieving an extremely large number of stable CRP space of $\sim 4 \times 10^{31}$.

articleTitle: A 200Gb/s, 3.5pJ/bit Monolithically Integrated WDM SiPhotonic Transceiver for Chiplet Optical I/O
abstract: Silicon photonics (SiPh) technology fabricates both electronic and photonic circuits on the same CMOS wafer, enabling the optical transceivers integrate into the xPU’s package as embedded I/O [1]. By directly attaching fiber to the chip edge, the interconnect reach is extended and the energy efficiency is significantly improved. Previous works have demonstrated the hybrid integration of separate electronic and photonic chips in different processes [2] [3] [4]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, hybrid integration inevitably introduces significant parasitic capacitance due to the presence of ESD and I/O pads, which degrade signal integrity and energy efficiency. Previous monolithic integration of micro-ring (MR) WDM transceivers has demonstrated that these issues can be effectively overcome, but their speed is limited to a maximum of 32Gbps/channel [5]. As transmission speeds increase, several issues arise, as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) To ensure the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the modulated signal and meet the input sensitivity requirements of the receiver (RX), the transmitter (TX) needs a higher extinction ratio (ER). This often requires the microring modulator (MRM) to be biased at a higher insertion loss(IL), leading to a non-linear and limited electro-optic(EO) response. (2) To reduce inter-channel crosstalk, the RX employs a sharp roll-off micro-ring resonator (MRR) to prevent spectral leakage from adjacent wavelengths. But narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM) can result in signals with insufficient bandwidth after demultiplexing.

articleTitle: A 300W 1.27kW/inch3 98.0% Peak Efficiency 48V-to-12V Switch Tank Converter Controller with Integrated Multilevel Driver and Adaptive ZCS On-time Control
abstract: Nowadays, there is a growing demand for high-power DC-DC converters with an input of 48 V intermediate bus voltage [1] –[5]. The intermediate bus voltage plays a crucial role in influencing system efficiency and power density. A high-efficiency $4: 1$ switch tank converter (STC) has been introduced as a solution. Traditional discrete approaches [1], [3] involve several external components for operation, which decrease power density. Considering the acceptable heat and integration level at 300 W -to-500W output power, maximizing the integration and power density is the contribution of this paper. Conventional cascaded bootstrap strategy results in a rapid decrease in bootstrap voltage in Fig. 1, where dual-path bootstrap gate driver has been proposed and Ron of the top power switch is still limited [5]. Moreover, the resonant frequencies of two tanks are not easily equivalent in Fig. 1, increasing the difficulty of implementing ZCS in both tanks. At a 48V DC bias, there is an almost 50% decrease in capacitance for X7R compared to C0G. These inherent properties lead to resonant tank mismatch and hard turn-off behavior when utilizing the cost-effective X7R. Traditional ZCS control can only avoid the switching noise by using large $\mathrm{V}_{\text {TH}}[6]$, which introduces obvious Poff2 loss at light load and deteriorates efficiency. However, for small $V_{T H}$ detection, additional $\Delta P_{\text {loss}}$ effect caused by the offset voltage Vos from the detector will be even worse. To address the above issues, this work proposed an integrated driver with high-precision ZCS control for a high-powerdensity $4: 1$ switch tank converter.

articleTitle: A 0.40pJ/Spike 10μs-Latency Asynchronous Spiking Neural Network with Compact Nonideality-Tolerating CIM-Synapses for Always-On Near-Sensor AI
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are suitable for always-on near-sensor AI [1]. Nevertheless, the temporal dimension complicates its IC implementation. Latency and power consumption increase with finer timing granularity in clock-driven circuits [2] [3]. A global-asynchronous local-synchronous SNN chip [4] still consumes $1.5 \mathrm{pJ} /$Spike and $100 \mathrm{~ms} / \mathrm{Inf}$. By combining SNN with Computing-In-Memory (CIM), the spike-driven Asynchronous Neuromorphic Inference Engine (ANIE) [5] has achieved fast inference ($40 \mu \mathrm{~s}$ latency). However, two major challenges exists (Fig. 1): 1) There is a lack of an end-to-end model that integrates noise-aware Feature Extraction (FE) and variation-aware inference, thereby avoiding perchip model-circuit calibrations. 2) Complex peripherals for precise signal control exist in CIM-synapses [1] [5] [6] to compensate circuit nonidealities, but degrade their efficiency.

articleTitle: An All-digital, 3.68 mV/LSB Voltage Sensor based Droop Prediction and Fast Mitigation System in 28nm CMOS
abstract: In digital SoCs, voltage droop caused by work-load variations can reduce the voltage by over 100 mV in about 10 ns [1]. However, to capture the details during the droop as shown in Fig. 1 top, previous voltage sensors still face challenges: 1) Their resolution is limited by the sensitivity of the standard cells in Voltage-to-Time Converter (VTC); 2) Low sampling rate and VTC is affected by PVT (Process, Voltage-nonlinear, Temperature) variations [2–5]. On the other hand, traditional LDOs struggle to effectively mitigate droop due to the loop-latency and the fine regulation strategy [6–10]. Current injection techniques have been proposed to address the droop issue, but they are still limited by the detection and control latency, and it is challenging to determine the precise amount of current to inject.

articleTitle: A Single/Dual-Output Switched-Capacitor DC-DC Converter with Geometrically Arranged Soft VCR Transitions
abstract: Dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) enhances power efficiency in digital systems, particularly in small loT devices with limited power sources. Switched-capacitor (SC) DC-DC converters offer several benefits, including high integrability and cost reduction, when implementing DVS in small systems [1]. Reconfigurable SC DC-DC converters with fine-grained voltage conversion ratios (VCRs) [2], [3] have efficient wide voltage ranges. Those featuring dual output [4], [5] can further reduce the area overhead for multiple dynamic loads. However, reconfigurable SC converters may encounter charge redistribution losses when the VCR changes (Fig. 1, top left). Reordering all serially connected stages in a converter [6] can help, but the complex switching network between flying capacitors makes it challenging to expand converter stages to achieve a fine-grained VCR transition.

articleTitle: An Energy-Efficient Composite Phase Shift 16-QAM Frequency Multiplying TX Achieving a 3.4% EVM in 65nm CMOS
abstract: Next-generation bioelectronic/loT devices demand highly-integrated wireless systems at extremely low cost and high energy efficiency, where the transmitter (TX) often dominates the overall power consumption, posing a major design challenge to the entire system. Although sub-GHz TXs with sub-mW power consumption have been reported recently [1–3], the simple modulation scheme (OOK, FSK, etc.) limits the spectral efficiency and data rate, while is not well-suited for applications, such as brain-computer interface, real time image transmission, etc. Therefore, a QAM architecture is usually desired with an expected data rate up to tens of Mbps. State-of-the art QAM-modulated sub-GHz TX architectures can be categorized as follow. Conventional direct-conversion architecture in Fig. 1(a) provides excellent error-tolerable performance at the expense of extra power/hardware overhead. The quadrature structure in [4] modulates phase/amplitude separately by leveraging a multi-phase PLL or injection-locked ring oscillator (ILRO) [Fig. 1(b)(c)], however, requires precise phase/amplitude control to achieve good error vector magnitude (EVM). In [5], the QAM signal is generated by combining two adjacent vectors through a RF-DAC in a polar-like structure. Despite extra power saving, it suffers from significant phase/amplitude mismatch and limited EVM. In this paper, we proposed an ultra-low power 16-QAM TX based on the composite phase shift (CPS) technique. The modulation scheme in this paper demonstrates excellent mismatch-resilient performance as analyzed in the following part, resulting in an improved EVM at the target data rate with high energy efficiency and low hardware overhead.

articleTitle: A 13-34 TOPS/W Edge-AI Processor Featuring Booth-Value-Confined Accelerator, Near-Memory Computing, and Contiguity-Aware Mapping
abstract: Recently, edge artificial intelligence (AI) devices, particularly those with in-memory-computing (IMC)/near-memory-computing (NMC) architecture, have demonstrated superior power efficiency compared with conventional von-Neumann architecture [1]–[7]. To further improve the power efficiency, approximate computing techniques have been investigated [8], which inevitably incur accuracy loss as such approximations cannot be evaluated during the NN training stage on GPU (Fig. 1). In addition, despite the exceptionally high power efficiency at the macro-level, the often-overlooked resource consumption for inter-/intra-layer data alignment and reshape can actually lead to substantial overhead of power consumption and latency. This is caused by 1) inefficient memory bandwidth utilization due to irregular or unbalanced read/write patterns (e.g., [3] [4]), and 2) severe memory space discontinuity due to inefficient neural network (NN) mapping strategy (e.g., [6] [7]), as shown in Fig. 1. Hence, when considering the end-to-end NN execution, aspects of off-chip memory traffic and network mapping strategy require further investigations at the architectural level.

articleTitle: A Non-contact TMR-Based Active Electrode for BCG Recording
abstract: Ballistocardiography (BCG) works as an effective diagnostic tool for various cardiac diseases, such as sleep disorder [1], and heart failure [2] by detecting reactionary forces through the body from heartbeats. Moreover, the combination of ECG and BCG recording can be used for continuous cuffless blood pressure measurement [3]. The comparison between ECG and BCG working scenarios is shown in Fig 1. The conventional ECG recording is based on contact sensing and requires extra wires and ground electrodes (for example, the DRL electrode and lead wires). While BCG recording is based on non-contact sensing, and there is no ground electrode needed. However, conventional BCG recording has its limitations. The foam factor of BCG sensors (the optical fiber or the piezoelectric sensor) is huge because of their limited sensitivity. The BCG sensor needs to cover the entire chest area to measure the mechanical movement and requires post-processing for BCG detection. The bulky sensors are usually integrated into the pillow or the mattress, which makes it difficult to use as wearable devices. Although some work proposed a wearable BCG sensor with MEMS accelerators used in ears [4], the work only achieves the J peak detection due to its low signal-tonoise ratio (SNR). To address the aforementioned issues, this paper presents the first-in-literature TMR-based active electrode for BCG recording. The active electrode consists of two custom-designed chips: the TMR chip (Chip 1) and the AFE chip (Chip 2). When placing the TMR-based active BCG electrode on the chest, the heartbeat causes the ballistic vibration, which leads to the geomagnetic change over the TMR sensor, and the signal fluctuation is amplified and digitized by the AFE chip finally.

articleTitle: A 320MHz BW NS TD-ADC Assisted C/DT Hybrid Pipelined ADC with SAB-based Residue Amplifying Filter
abstract: With the advent of WLAN technologies, over 320 MHz BW and $\gt 65 \mathrm{~dB}$ DR ADCs become indispensable to support newly developed WiFi standards. Three classic solutions can reach the said targets but involve various compromises (Fig. 1 top). CT MASH ADCs [1] rely on a relatively high OSR $(\geqslant 7)$ as well as NS order to accommodate the adequate noise spectral density (NSD), limiting the energy efficiency. The CT pipeline (PIPE) ADC [2–3] obviates the feedback loop and its 1st stage energy effectively provides preliminary quantization, residue generation, amplification, and filtering. However, the backend CT quantization can be power-hungry [2] [4]. The DT NS pipeline ADC offers a low-power alternative [5] but loses the intrinsic anti-aliasing (AA) ability from its CT counterparts. This work hybridizes CT and DT NS PIPE, gaining the pros from the CT PIPE front-end and DT PIPE backend. Together with the Single amplifier biquad (SAB) - Residue Amplifying Filter (RAF) and NS TD-QTZ, the C/DT PIPE ADC demonstrates superior energy efficiency over CT MASH ADCs with 320MHz BW.

articleTitle: A 0.036mm2 80Mb/s-to-15.96Gb/s C-PHY and D-PHY Combo Receiver with Background Calibrations in 4nm FinFET
abstract: Mobile industry processor interface (MIPI) C-PHY and D-PHY have been widely used in various applications for multiple cameras, dual display, and automotive. Especially, C-PHY interface has been attracting solution to deliver expansive bandwidth due to its 3-level coding gain of 2.28bit/symbol over three-wired trio [1]. The sampling clock at receiver is recovered from the clock-embedded trio signal, thus no additional clock lane is required. However, 3-level transitions induce the additional switching jitter which degrades the eye-openings. Also it causes the clock recovery error that the multiple clock edges occur within 1UI period. To recover only one clock edge in 1 UI period, the transition masking range should be calibrated to be around 0.35 UI [1]. To enhance the interface speed more, it is necessary to reduce the skew among trio and to compensate for channel loss. Compared to C-PHY, D-PHY does not need the complex circuits such as encoder/decoder and clock recovery. So, some products for low data bandwidth prefer to use D-PHY rather than C-PHY. To operate according to various bandwidth requirements with the same hardware, developing a combo-type architecture for C-PHY and D-PHY is necessary. In this work, we develop the $80 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s}-\mathrm{to}-15.96 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ C/D-PHY combo receiver which follows MIPI C-PHY v2.1 and D-PHY v2.5 standard [2]. In addition, this work proposes the background calibrations to correct the deterministic skew among wires and to compensate for frequency dependent terms including C-PHY transition masking range and equalizer.

articleTitle: A 26.5-to-29.5GHz Transformer-Based Doherty Phased-Array Transceiver Front-End With 7-Bit Phase Shifter and 16% Back-Off Drain Efficiency
abstract: Millimeter-wave (mm-wave) phased-array transceivers (TRXs) with beamforming techniques are extensively utilized in 5G wireless communication systems to mitigate significant free space path loss. However, as the scale of the phased array and data rate increases, it encounters two major challenges. Firstly, the phase shifting scan range and resolution must meet the requirements of beam steering resolution [1, 2]. Secondly, the system efficiency, particularly in the power back-off (PBO) efficiency, needs to be improved due to the high peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) of the quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) signals.

articleTitle: A Real-Time Optical-Flow-based SLAM FPGA Accelerator with Inter-Frame Similarity Exploitation and Correlation-Guided Mixed-Precision Flow Update
abstract: Recently, the increasing demands of scene understanding and precise spatial mapping have driven Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) more crucial in robotics for estimating the trajectory and the structure of the environment [1–2]. Previous feature-based SLAM processors [3–5] retrieve pose and 3D maps by tracking limited feature points $({\lt}5 k)$, making them vulnerable to changing environments and illumination. In addition, feature-based SLAM cannot directly construct dense maps, impairing their applicability in advanced robotics. In contrast, optical-flow-based SLAM (OpFSLAM) [6] fully utilizes pixel-level information to provide continuous motion estimations and generate dense map representations, meeting the diverse requirements of emerging mobile robots. An overview of OpF-SLAM is shown in Fig. 1, which involves extracting per-pixel feature and context information, constructing correlation volume (Corr) for all pixel pairs, iteratively updating optical flow, estimating the camera trajectory, and building environment maps.However, OpF-SLAM encounters several challenges in achieving real-time (>30fps) tracking, as shown in Fig. 1: (1) The data dependency between feature extraction and correlation construction causes latency overhead. (2) Iterative optical flow updates require an excessive computational amount, accounting for 62.19% of the total computation.

articleTitle: RMMIC: A 40 μW Reconfigurable Multi-modal Multi-channel Interface Circuit System for Bio-signals Monitoring
abstract: Monitoring our multi-biological signals (bio-signals) provides us with a holistic view of our physiological condition (Figure 1). With increasing demand for integrating multiple bio-signals into a single chip, it is imperative to address multiple design challenges for efficient multi-modal biosensor acquisition [1]. The bio-signals include bio-potential signals (ExG), photo-plethysmography signals (PPG), and bio-impedance signals (BioZ) that are all unique in their electric properties (voltage, current, and resistance), have a large dynamic range ($4 \times$ order magnitudes in frequency and amplitude), and have a tremendous amount of variation among channels (middle of the Figure 1). The challenge of amplifying and quantizing diverse in-band bio-signals with a single signal acquisition circuit has attracted significant attention among researchers [2–6].

articleTitle: A 1.3mW 10MHz-BW 71dB-SNDR Two-Step TDC-Assisted Continuous-Time Noise-Shaping SAR ADC
abstract: NS-SAR ADCs have been a popular choice in various applications due to their excellent power efficiency. Many NS-SAR ADCs have been based on discrete-time (DT) operations (Fig. 1(top)), leading to two critical issues: 1) The kT/C noise from the sampling operation sets the fundamental SNR limit of the ADC. Hence, to achieve a higher SNR, the input sampling capacitor must be increased, posing more power burdens to the input and reference buffers. 2) A strong anti-aliasing filter is required because their STF is unity across all frequency bands. To address these challenges, the design recently reported in [1] demonstrates the feasibility of applying CT operation to the NS-SAR ADC (Fig. 1(middle)). Nevertheless, several challenges still remain: 1) The stride of the ADC’s input DAC decreases at a binary pace as the conversion continues, thus inducing input-dependent errors (EIN). As the number of CT SAR quantizer bits is increased to gain more resolution, $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{IN}}$ also increases accordingly, limiting the resolution [2]. 2) The input to the integrator, the residue signal, cannot be available due to its drastic changes during SAR conversion ($\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\text {SAR}}$). This leads to the adoption of a duty-cycled integrator that directs the loop filter input to a virtual ground, thus losing the integration information during $\phi_{\text {SAR}}$. As a result, the system becomes unstable, and the signal transfer function (STF) and noise transfer function (NTF) are degraded if the condition that the proportion of TSAR within T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">s</inf> becomes significantly small (less than 5%) can not be guaranteed. Therefore, this limitation makes the design of high-speed CT NS- SAR ADC so challenging.

articleTitle: A 6.4Gb/s/pin HBM3 Digital PHY with Low-Power, Area-Efficient Techniques for Chiplet-Based AI processors in 12-nm CMOS
abstract: Since the emergence of artificial neural networks, we are currently experiencing a wave of transformation centered around generative Al models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. In response to these changes, there is a growing demand for low-power and highspeed memory to facilitate the real-time processing of large-scale data such as images, videos, and texts. In the industry, high-performance AI chips utilizing high-bandwidth memory (HBM) are being developed [1], [2]. Particularly, next-generation AI processors tend to adopt a chiplet-based architecture consisting of HBM and NPUs [3]–[5]. With improvements in HBM performance, the operating frequency of HBM3 has increased by approximately three times compared to the previous HBM2E, rising from 1.2 GHz to 3.2 GHz. As a result, it has become crucial to implement a digital physical layer (digital PHY) capable of processing data at high speeds.

articleTitle: A 28-nm 141.4TOPS/W Scalable Reconfigurable Deep Learning SoC for Large-Scale Neural Networks
abstract: Devices empowered by Al have brought tremendous benefits to humanity.
