Fig. 1 shows diverse applications, such as convolutional neural network (CNN) for environmental sensing, graph convolutional network (GCN) for social network analysis, and transformer for natural language processing. Al accelerators have been developed to tackle the increased computational complexity and versatile network structures. Hardware parallelism is applied to improve the throughput for neural network (NN) processing [1–3]. However, hardware parallelism for a specific network structure leads to decreased chip utilization. There has been a surge in the scale of NNs to improve the AI performance. Multi-chip solutions are promising to support large-scale NNs [1–4]. In the distributive multichip designs [1] [4], data for one single layer are partitioned into tensors along a single dimension and processed across multiple chips. This results in high data movement across chips. A chip may also receive insufficient data due to improper distribution, making it infeasible to support one complex layer (with more neurons). In the cascaded multi-chip designs [2] [3], a chip with uni-directional dataflow must await completion of operations by the subsequent chips. This causes low hardware utilization for the multi-chip system, which makes mapping deeper neural networks (with more layers) on multiple chips inefficient (or even infeasible), given limited on-chip memories.

articleTitle: A 1.27-mW Battery-Powered Multimodal Biosensor Interface IC for Wireless Motion Intention Recognition in Wearable Robots
abstract: Wearable robots augment human capabilities across diverse sectors, including healthcare, industry, and the military. In particular, walking assistance exoskeletons aid individuals suffering from reduced mobility. An accurate motion intention recognition system offers precise assistance in using wearable robots, helping adapt to individual movement patterns to enhance the robot’s operation efficiency and the user’s convenience.

articleTitle: A 105.8dB A-weighted DR CT Delta-Sigma Audio ADC Using Current-Steering DAC Current Recycling Amplifier
abstract: Continuous-time (CT) delta-sigma modulators (DSMs) are attractive for audio ADCs due to their reduced bandwidth requirements of the op-amps and free to kT/C noise limitations as compared to the discrete-time (DT) counterparts. In these CT-DSMs, resistive DACs and current-steering DACs are widely used but the latter have advantages of better linearity characteristics and higher power supply rejection ratio (PSRR) without dedicated low-dropout regulator (LDO).

articleTitle: A 19.58-to-21.38-GHz Low-Power Quad-Core VCO with Compact 3rd-Order Q-boost Inductors Achieving -191.8-dBc/Hz FoM and -205.4-dBc/Hz FoMA
abstract: In the Internet-of-Things (loT) applications, such as human sensors, robots, and vehicles, which are battery-dependent, optimal mm-Wave-based sensing requires a frequency source with low power consumption, miniaturization, and high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) [1]. This necessitates a low-jitter and low-power phase-locked loop (PLL). To minimize jitter within a given PLL power budget, balancing power allocation between the loop and the voltage control oscillators (VCO) is required [2]. Since the thermal region phase noise (PN) of VCO dictates the out-band PN of the PLL, it is essential to suppress thermal region PN with a low VCO power budget. Meanwhile, compact size is also significant for low-cost loT applications, hence requiring inductor shrinkage. However, optimizing PN, power, and area simultaneously in traditional single-core VCOs is challenging [3–5], mainly owing to the design trade-off of the inductor between inductance, Q factor, and area. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (middle), designing an inductor with a large L and high Q is highly desirable because the former helps to reduce VCO power while the latter is essential for low PN. Two widely used inductor topologies are presented in Fig. 1 (bottom). The single-coil inductor exhibits a high Q because the large distance between the two sides of the coil causes negligible self-canceling; yet, it is area-inefficient for large L designs. The multi-coil inductor offers a high L with a compact size but suffers from degraded Q caused by the severe self-canceling and parasitic effects, due to the narrow distance between the sides of the coils.

articleTitle: A Compact Optical Image Stabilization Chip with Actuator Trackability Improvement Controller and Double Offset Cancel Hall Amplifier to Improve Camera Shake Correction.
abstract: Image stabilization technique is a very effective way of capturing clear movie and is widely used in cameras, smartphones, wearable cameras, etc. There are two main types of image stabilization techniques: Electronic Image Stabilization (EIS), which uses digital image processing, and Optical Image Stabilization (OIS), which stabilizes the optical axis by physically correcting the position of the image sensor or lens. EIS is low cost because no additional parts are required. But if the image before correction is unclear, correction effect is limited [1]. Therefore, OIS is mainly used. Many of the CMOS image sensor(CIS) installed in recent smartphones easily exceed 10 million pixels. But, the higher the resolution of the CIS, the more serious the image blur caused by camera shake. In addition, the influence of camera shake become even more noticeable during long exposure shooting or zoom shooting. Therefore, further improvements of camera shake correction are required. To realize them, it is necessary to (1) accurately detect the position of the sensor and lens, and accurately calculate the target position for correction, and (2) move the sensor and lens to the target position with high accuracy using an actuator. However, there are the following issues. One is that the detection accuracy decreases due to interference between the detection elements. The other is that the actuator is affected by frictional forces, it is difficult to track the target position, especially when starting to move. In addition, when higher resolution is attempted to improve calculation accuracy, the influence of noise which generated in the analog blocks or caused by mutual interference between analog blocks, and the influence of the variation of AD-conversion error caused by PWM signal using PWM driver become apparent at converting analog signals from detection elements into digital signals, and countermeasures against analog noise are required. Furthermore, from the perspective of commercialization, it is also important to realize a smaller chip to reduce the chip cost. In addition, it is important to achieve more stable and practical performance in the industrial field, but there are few examples of academic analysis of OIS to achieve this. To overcome the above issues and further improve camera shake correction, we propose a compact OIS IC shown in Fig. 1 that applies the following three noble techniques: (1) an Actuator Trackability Improvement Controller (ATIC), (2) a Double Offset Cancel Hall Amplifier (DOC-HA), and (3) a Pulse width modulation Noise Suppression ADC (PNS-ADC).

articleTitle: A Single-Channel 3.1GS/s 45dB SNDR Pipelined ADC using Amplify-and-Select Structure in 28nm CMOS
abstract: A high-speed single-channel ADC is a key building block in highly-parallel TIADCs with sampling rates far beyond tens of GS/s. A faster single-channel reduces the number of channels for the same aggregate sample rate, simplifying design and lowering costs. Traditionally, flash ADCs [1] are the fastest structure but suffer from severe area and power penalties even for medium resolution. Time domain ADCs [2] recently demonstrated multi-GS/s conversion rates, but have yet to surpass limited linearity and PVT sensitivity. Pipelined ADCs are commonly used for balanced performance between speed and linearity, but the conventional design based upon the sequential processes limits itself from reaching higher speed. Prior work [3] tried to break this speed bottleneck by allowing a parallel run of operations using a post-amplification residue generation scheme. This work presents an amplify-and-select stage structure to overcome the speed limitation of the conventional pipelined ADC along with a replica-biased supply-regulation scheme that keeps the common-mode and gain characteristics of dynamic amplifier consistent, which is necessary for the ADC linearity calibration. The prototype ADC at $3.1 \mathrm{GS} / \mathrm{s}$ achieves an effective resolution of 7.28 b over a range of temperatures with state-of-the-art FoMs of 153.7 dB.

articleTitle: An Area-Efficient PVT-Dependent Adaptive Assist Termination Technique with SNM Detector for High Density SRAM
abstract: This paper presents an area-efficient assist architecture using a static noise margin (SNM) detector for high-density (HD) SRAMs that are particularly vulnerable to process variation. The SNM detector is arranged in the peripheral and composed of a logic SRAM cell with simple small logic circuits that is designed to be a replica of the least stable cell in order to reproduce the worst SNM characteristics. By using this detector, unneeded assist can be eliminated depending on PVT conditions, as a result, dramatical improvement of access time (25%) and reduction of active power (24.4% @ write and 32.8% @read) are achieved with the smallest area overhead (0.015%).

articleTitle: A Fully Integrated 4:1 DC-DC Converter Using Electromagnetically Coupled Class-D LC Oscillators Achieving 74.5% Peak Efficiency and 0.78W/mm² Peak Power Density
abstract: Fully integrated DC-DC converters enable direct power supply to integrated circuits (ICs) from DC sources such as battery or USB ports. However, a high conversion ratio is necessary since the DC power sources’ voltage is much higher than that required by the ICs. Achieving a high conversion ratio unfortunately results in a significant degradation in performance, including power density and efficiency, due to increased power transfer steps or high voltage switch drivers. To overcome these challenges, a couple of research efforts have been introduced recently. In [4], an integrated converter using a resonant switched capacitor technique is proposed, which achieves a $3: 1$ conversion ratio with a high efficiency of 78.3%. However, it suffers from a low power density of $16 \mathrm{~mW} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ due to a low switching frequency of 30 MHz. In [5], an on-chip DC-DC converter based on electromagnetically coupled LC oscillators (EMLC) is introduced, which achieves a high power density of $4.1 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$. Unfortunately, it is restricted to conversion ratios of 2:1 or 1:2 and exhibits a low efficiency of 60.4% at peak power density.

articleTitle: A Hybrid-Resonance Single-Stage Dual-Output Rectifier With High Voltage Difference for Wireless Power Transfer System
abstract: Wireless power transfer systems have been widely used in implantable medical devices (IMDs). In these systems, multiple supplies are required to power different modules. Generally, a high voltage is used for electrical stimulation, and a low voltage is used for power-hungry circuits including digital signal processor (DSP), telemetry, etc. In prior works, dual-output rectifiers have been well-established to meet the requirement for IMDs, and there are several typical structures. For example, a dual-output rectifier achieves two outputs by adding DC-DC converters in series with the rectifier. However, this structure occupies a large area and the cascade structure greatly reduces the receiver efficiency. Therefore, single-stage dual-output rectifiers (SSDORs) have been widely studied to reduce size and increase efficiency. In [1], a parallel-resonance full-bridge rectifier is proposed to generate dual outputs, but power transistors up to 6 are required. In [2], a series-resonance half-bridge rectifier with 4 transistors is proposed to achieve dual outputs. However, the existing methods are not capable of obtaining two voltages with a large voltage difference. Series-resonance is more appropriate to transfer high power and parallel-resonance is easier to generate a high output voltage [2]. Therefore, a hybrid-resonance rectifier is very suitable for IMDs.

articleTitle: A 97.1% Buck-Boost Battery Charger with a Constant Current Extension Technique for 2x Faster Battery Charging with Accurate Termination of Charging Process
abstract: With portable devices requiring more power and efficiency, there is an increasing demand for larger battery capacities and faster charging solutions [1]. The battery charging process comprises three stages: pre-charge, constant current (CC), and constant voltage (CV). The conventional charging profile is depicted at the top of Fig. 1. Achieving fast charging depends on the transition point from CC to CV mode. The built-in resistance detection (BIRD) technique can efficiently extend CC mode and reduce CV mode duration, thereby shortening the charging time [2–3]. However, the accuracy of BIRD is limited due to variations in the built-in resistor $\left(R_{B I R}\right)$ with temperature and state of charge (SOC) changes. Consequently, the inaccuracies introduced by BIRD result in an extended CV duration. Simultaneously, the conventional architecture faces challenges in accurately distinguishing between small charging current and termination current due to noise, resulting in premature termination and inefficiency in CV mode. Insufficient charging will significantly reduce battery capacity, with just 0.1 V of undercharging, a 4.2 V lithium-ion battery will cause a 10% capacity loss [4]. Therefore, the proposed constant current extension (CCE) technique introduces additional CC time in CV mode to reduce $C V$ charging time for fast charging and ensure high efficiency and accurate termination time.

articleTitle: A cryogenic pulse shaper for spin qubit control utilizing 1ns-time-resolution ADCs on an active silicon interposer operating at sub-100 mK temperatures
abstract: Spin quantum bits (qubits) in semiconductor silicon quantum dots are one of the most promising candidates for large-scale quantum processor units, since they potentially have higher scalability through advanced semiconductor integration technologies. However, spin qubits require many control signals such as bias voltages, pulses and high-frequency microwaves, which is a major barrier to scale-up of qubits. In current small-scale quantum computer setup, the spin qubits inside the 100 mK cold finger of dilution refrigerator have been controlled by external room temperature instruments via long cables as shown in the left image of Fig. 1. This setup, consisting of fully analog signal transmission between qubits and external instruments, degrades the signal integrity and causes heat injection via cables, making it unsuitable for scalable qubits. Thus, cryogenic CMOS controller solutions have been widely developed to control the qubits from inside the refrigerator by installing the signal generation circuits on 4 K plate as depicted in the middle image of Fig. 1 [1]. This allows for the connection from the external devices to the refrigerator to be made with only digital wirings, which reduces number of cables and heat inflow. However, the distance between the 4 K plate and the 100 mK cold finger is still more than 2 m, degrading the integrity of wideband signals such as pulses.

articleTitle: An 8.1-to-353 TOPS/W Energy-Aware Deep-Learning Accelerator Supporting Dynamic Neural Networks
abstract: The demand for edge Al is rapidly increasing in various applications, including image classification, object detection, image segmentation, and key-point detection. Conventionally, deep-learning accelerators are designed for a fixed operating scenario, targeting a high accuracy with affordable energy consumption. However, the operating scenarios and performance requirements may vary. There are cases where low-energy operation is the first priority and a slight accuracy loss is tolerated. Therefore, an energy-aware solution supporting a variety of operating scenarios is required.

articleTitle: A -60 to 145 °C, 216 fJ·K2 Energy-Efficient MOS-Based Temperature Sensor Achieving 71.8 mK Resolution
abstract: Energy-efficient temperature sensors are essential for on-chip temperature monitoring. To measure temperature, they convert temperature into electrical signals using devices such as MOSFETs [1], [2], BJTs [3], and resistors [4], [5]. MOS-based temperature sensors have low energy consumption because of their compact structures, but the energy efficiency has been relatively worse compared to recent resistor-based sensors. However, this low energy efficiency is not due to the intrinsic limitation of MOS devices. This paper optimizes the temperature conversion method and overall sensor design to improve the energy efficiency of MOS-based temperature sensors.

articleTitle: A Compact D-Band Phase Shifter with 0.1-degree Phase Resolution and 0.8-degree RMS Phase Error in 65 nm CMOS
abstract: Sub-THz phased-array transceivers play an important role in future 6th-generation mobile communication systems (6G). In particular, the phase shifter is an essential circuit for phased-array transceivers. The phase shifter must have high-resolution phase steps and low phase error to achieve high-precision beam steering and calibration [1]. This work presents a high-precision D-band cascaded phase shifter for 6 G wireless communications. The active fine-tuning phase shifter with feedback technology realizes high-resolution phase shifting. This technology achieves over three times the fine phase shift of conventional works with lower power consumption. In addition, a compact propagation delay phase shifter using a non-uniform architecture is proposed. Thanks to this technique, a 360-degree phase shift with low phase error and reduced insertion loss is realized. The proposed phase shifter achieves a phase step of 0.1° and RMS phase error of 0.8° within the frequency range of 150-160 GHz. The power consumption is 5 mW, and the IC core area is $0.099 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$, fabricated in a 65 nm CMOS process.

articleTitle: Where do Innovations stem from?: Further Innovations Beyond Silicon Technology
abstract: The early semiconductor industry focused on the development of monolithic devices through technological innovations in silicon-based processes and devices. This 1st Wave of innovation resulted in greater chip integration, rapid performance improvements, and reduced costs, thereby expanding the semiconductor ecosystem and ushering in the era of productivity innovation. Subsequently, the emergence of new IT devices such as PCs and smartphones resulted from the co-optimization of hardware and software technologies, enabling the creation of diverse applications. As a 2nd Wave, this highlighted the need for high-performance computing and networking to process big data, a byproduct of internet connectivity. Consequently, it accelerated the development of parallel computing architectures, high-speed memory, high-speed interfaces, and IC packaging technologies. As a result, the artificial intelligence industry experienced rapid growth, and the demand for high-performance semiconductor products surged. Despite these efforts, achieving IC performance often necessitates larger chip sizes, which produce more heat. This requires additional countermeasures that drive up costs. Recently, the semiconductor industry has shown a trend towards actively using advanced process such as Gate-All-Around (GAA) nanosheet transistor to develop ultra-deep integration ICs with lower power consumption and heat dissipation. However, these advanced processes lead to “Technology Inflation”, pushing many semiconductor products to use these sophisticated processes and “Cost Inflation” due to exponentially increasing development expenses, thereby diminishing the significance of Moore’s Law and reducing development efficiency. Furthermore, the consolidation of IP and EDA tool markets by some EDA vendors exacerbates cost inflation by inducing support for advanced processes in existing EDA workflows. To mitigate the current technology and cost inflation in the semiconductor industry and enable the development of reasonably priced and technologically sound products, innovation through diversity is necessary. This 3rd Wave involves breaking down the boundaries between various technological domains and fostering an environment where new companies can compete freely.

articleTitle: TID-Tolerant StrongARM Comparator and Sampling Network for Satellite Application High-Voltage ADCs
abstract: Semiconductor devices for satellite applications must be robust in irradiation environments, up to 100 krad of total ionizing dose (TID) over a 10-year space mission [1]. While low-voltage (LV) processes exhibit higher TID resilience owing to their thin gate oxide (Gox) (<10 nm) [2], highvoltage (HV) circuits such as ADCs required for various monitoring purposes in satellites still require solutions to the TID-induced threshold $\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}\right)$ shift problem: trapped holes by TID in NMOS gate oxide decrease $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}$ (whereas $\left|\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}\right|$ in PMOS increases). Fig. 1 illustrates this phenomenon along with the equivalent circuit model. $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}$ shift $\left(\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}, \mathrm{TID}}\right)$ is modeled with a voltage source on the gate and the additional leakage path through the field oxide (Fox) is modeled with a lumped NMOS, Mn,Fox. From our TID test, $\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}, \mathrm{TID}}$ of an NMOS in our $0.35 \mu \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{HV}$ CMOS technology is measured to be 1.5 V and 2.5 V at the TID levels of 50 krad (TID-1) and 100 krad (TID-2), respectively. To consider even worse case scenarios, $\Delta \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}, \mathrm{TID}}$ is extrapolated as 3 V (TID-3) and 4 V (TID-4). It is worth to note that our HV NMOS switches cannot be turned off even at TID-1 level because its typical $\mathrm{V}_{T H}$ is 1.48 V, while $\left|\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}\right|$ increase in PMOS benignly reduces their on conductance (gon).

articleTitle: WhiteDwarf: 12.24 TFLOPS/W 40 nm Versatile Neural Inference Engine for Ultra-Compact Execution of CNNs and MLPs Through Triple Unstructured Sparsity Exploitation and Triple Model Compression
abstract: Although over-parameterization grants neural networks high accuracy in various inference tasks, it also curses them with an exploding computational cost. It is known that these giant models can be sparsified without much loss in performance [1], but to achieve high execution efficiency, they should be condensed as much as possible without hampering the ongoing growth of neural model diversity. This paper presents the following holistic ultracompact approach towards this challenge, as illustrated in Fig. 1, using CNNs and MLPs for the demonstration of its effectiveness: triple model compression utilizing (1) network compression using the Folding technique [2]; (2) a method for concurrent training, pruning, and quantization based on the Multicoated Supermask (M-Sup) algorithm [3, 4]; and (3) adaptive precision with INT2-4 weights, FP8 activations, and FP16 normalization [5]. The proposed WhiteDwarf architecture features (4) off-chip access reduction with Huffmanen-coded weights; (5) triple unstructured sparsity exploitation on a 1 K Processing Element (PE) Tensor, exploiting the high sparsity of activations and weights (Fig. 1, right-top) with a non-zero gathering datapath, and the bit-level sparsity of weights with a bit-serial decomposition of multiplication; and (6) broad support of models via a hybrid controller with a custom RISC-V processor. On ImageNet, we compress a ResNet-50 (RN50) to 5.7% of the original memory size while maintaining 74.7% accuracy, and on CIFAR-100, we compress an MLP-Mixer [6] S24 (MS24) to 0.6% of the original without accuracy loss (see Fig. 4).

articleTitle: A PUF-Integrated Power Amplifier with Harmonic Tunable Matching Network-Controlled Spectral Regrowth Technique for RF Fingerprinting in IoT
abstract: loT security has become indispensable and much expected in future wireless networks. A physical layer authentication method called Radio Frequency Fingerprinting (RFF) had been realized through manufacturing process variation [1]. Following which, Q. Zhou et al. proposed the Physical Unclonable Function (PUF)-controlled RFF Power Amplifier (PA) as shown in Fig. 1(a) [2]. This design converted the digital fingerprint from PUF to DAC, and apply it to a PA through tuning the bias voltage to enable random distribution of the Out-ofBand Leakage Power (OOBLP) as unique identity tags. However, such bias control resulted in large In-Band Power (IBP) variation while OOBLP tuning, hence limited its actual applications. Besides, the absolute power of OOBLP is adopted to evaluate the identification error rate, which is channel-dependent and not effective when the signals passed through different paths with different channel losses. To address the above issues, this paper presents a PA integrated with a proposed ultra-low native Bit Error Rate (BER) PUF for RFF application. A harmonic tunable matching network (HTMN) is proposed to achieve a stable IBP when the out-of-band spectrum regrows (Fig. 1(b)). The power difference between OOBLP and IBP ($\triangle$ Power = OOBLP -IBP) is adopted to evaluate the identification error rate to avoid the multipath influence on OOBLP. Compared to the biasing method, the proposed RFF PA with HTMN stabilizes the fundamental output impedance and controls the $2^{\text {nd }}$ harmonic output impedance to realize a very large spectral regrowth tuning and achieve a constant IBP. A 2.4-GHz RFF PA integrated with proposed Static Random-Access Memory (SRAM) PUF is fabricated in $65-\mathrm{nm}$ CMOS process. It has only 0.16 dB maximum IBP variation when the OOBLP changing from -50.8 dBm to -35 dBm with a $2 \mathrm{Mb} / \mathrm{s} \pi / 4-$ DQPSK signal. The identification error rate of 96 data from six chips is only 1.46%.

articleTitle: A W-band Omnidirectional FMCW Radar with 18.18dBm Pout 6.76dB NF 52dB Isolation for 4.7cm Resolution and 10m Detection Distance
abstract: The frequency modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radars at sub-terahertz have gained significant attention in short-distance sensing due to their high resolution. To prevent receiver (Rx) saturation during continuous wave (CW) operation, it is imperative for FMCW radars to achieve high isolation between the transmitter (Tx) and Rx in the front-end. As demonstrated in [1], a 140GHz CMOS FMCW monostatic radar achieves 3.54cm resolution imaging and 33.3dB of total TRx isolation through an adaptive self-interference cancellation technique. To further improve the TRx isolation, a single-antenna TRx SoC featuring continuous-time adaptive leakage cancellation is proposed to achieve 40 dB isolation [2]. However, the detection range, and detection angle of these FMCW radars pose challenges in meeting requirements of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) radar. The integrated micro-system using multiple TRx-chips with array antennas is used to significantly enhance the detection range with relatively low resolution [3, 4]. A monostatic and bistatic G-band radar based on TRXs with on-chip antennas is presented, which exhibits 2.1cm resolution and 40dB isolation with limited detection angle and range [5]. Hence, the current FMCW radar is hard to meet the requirements for high resolution, extensive detection range, and wide angle simultaneously.

articleTitle: A 14.7mW Blocker-Tolerant Wideband Receiver Using a Transformer-Based N-Path Passive-LNA and a 2nd-Order TIA Achieving 110MHz RF-BW and 13dBm OB-IIP3
abstract: To underpin high-speed wireless communication in the sub-6GHz bands, especially for the 5G New Radio (NR) and towards the 6G standards, RF receivers (RXs) are evolved to support a wide signal bandwidth (BW) (e.g. 100MHz in 5G-NR), cover a wide RF spectrum, and become more resilience to out-of-band (OB) blockers. In [1], the mixer-first RX (Fig. 1, upper) supports a wide range of RF and has a high linearity (27 dBm OB-IIP3) by delaying the signal amplification to baseband (BB). This topology yet sacrifices the NF $(5.5 \mathrm{~dB})$ and power consumption $(60 \mathrm{~mW})$ due to no RF gain. In [2], the LNTA-based RX (Fig. 1, upper) attains a better tradeoff between NF (2.2dB) and power consumption (40 mW) with an RF gain, but at the expense of linearity (5 dBm OB-IIP3) and active area $\left(0.8 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}\right.$). In [3], the gainboosted N-path mixer-first RX (Fig. 1, lower) exhibits 2.9dB NF and 8 dBm OB-IIP3 with only 11 mW power consumption. Yet, the RF passband BW is limited to $\sim 4 \mathrm{MHz}$, hindering its applications on the standards such as 5G-NR. In addition, the RF coverage of the RXs [1]–[3] is limited by the input capacitance.

articleTitle: A 1.92nJ/Conv Pulse-Width Locked-Loop Time Domain Readout IC with VCO-Integrator and Pipeline TDC for Wheatstone Bridge Wearable Strain Sensing System
abstract: The Wheatstone bridge (WhB) is widely used as resistive sensor interfaces, commonly applied in pressure [1], temperature [2], strain [3] sensing systems. Conventional voltage domain WhB (VDWhB) shown in Fig.1(a) requires high performance OTA and large input RCs to reduce power and readout error at the cost of significant area penalty and design complexity. Recently, time domain bridge-to-digital converter (BDC) using a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) to convert resistance into frequency has gained significant attention [4] [Fig. 1(b)]. However, the open-loop structure of VCO-based systems limits the gain accuracy and linearity, which can be improved by embedding the VCO in a frequency-locked loop (FLL) based readout [3, 5] [Fig. 1(c)]. Nevertheless, VCO is power-hungry (about 50% of the entire system [3]) as the accumulated jitter has to be suppressed to improve readout accuracy. Additionally, large off-chip capacitors ($\gt10 \mathrm{nF}$) are still required which cannot be readily integrated on-chip [3], [5]. Furthermore, the oversampling time-to-digital converter (OSTDC) adds power overhead while preventing its application from systems with aggressive duty-cycling. To address these issues, we propose a time-domain readout circuit utilizing a VCO-based integrator (VCO-INT) enabled pulse-width locked loop (PWLL) and a Nyquist-rate multi-stage 10-bit pipeline TDC, as illustrated in Fig. 1(d) The overall readout circuit features a digitally-intensive structure with excellent energy efficiency and flexibility.

articleTitle: A 0.04 μJ/ Classification High-Accuracy Energy-Efficient ECG Processor with SNN On-Chip Backpropagation and Adaptive Threshold Encoding

For wearable edge devices, the two most important factors are power consumption and inference accuracy [1]. For power consumption, many previous works have adopted spiking neural networks (SNN) to improve energy efficiency.
