articleTitle: 22-nm Data Backup SRAM Using 3.3V IO MOSs with Ultralow-Voltage-Drop Erasure Technique for Secure IoT Applications
abstract: A new erasure technique in terms of ultralow voltage drop is proposed for data backup SRAM (DBRAM). After a tampering event is detected, the proposed macro erases all of the data stored in cells for a short period equivalent to 3 cycles with the same peak current as that of the normal SRAM read and write operations. As a result, the DBRAM can achieve erasure function even in a limited power supply condition such as battery-operated loT devices. The power performances and peak current characteristics are computationally analyzed and experimentally verified using the fabricated test chips in 22 nm CMOS process.

articleTitle: A 43.3 bit/cycle Inflate Accelerator Featuring Static-Dynamic Huffman Decoder with Multiple Checkpoints and Optimized End-Of-Block Control for Hyperscale data
abstract: Today’s explosively growing data volumes and the high storage cost make compression crucial for the Big Data industry. Deflate is a widely used lossless compression format that incorporates the LZ77 algorithm, which replaces repeated character strings with <length, distance> pairs, and the Huffman algorithm, which recodes characters based on their frequency of occurrence. The decoding process for a deflate-encoded file is called inflate. The decompression speed is critical, as stored data are typically compressed once but repeatedly decompressed for use in data processing systems. Consequently, strategies have been developed to enhance the decompression speed of inflate. The main challenge in improving inflate throughput lies in the data dependencies that invalidate parallel operations in Huffman decoding. Some studies [1], [2] have modified the deflate format to eliminate these data dependencies and achieve parallelism, but this approach results in incompatibility with existing inflate implementations. A speculative Huffman decoder for the GZIP decompressor, as proposed in [3], improves parallelism, resulting in a 69% increase in throughput. However, a single index checkpoint cannot ensure the success of the speculative thread (ST), which affects inflate throughput. Additionally, the ST stops when it encounters an end-of-block (EOB) marker and only restarts after the primary thread (PT) meets an EOB, limiting the ST’s efficiency. When Huffman decoding is accelerated, the throughput of the LZ77 decoder may become the critical path. The LZ77 decoder can be parallelized using a two-pass method. Other approaches [4], [5] cyclically partition the history buffer to access multiple memory locations simultaneously.

articleTitle: A 28nm CMOS 12-bit-600-MS/s 15.6mW Pipelined ADC with Two-Stage Gainboosting FIA-based RA
abstract: Pipelined ADCs have been a preferred architecture for high-resolution and high-speed applications [1], [2]. In typical pipelined ADCs, the residue amplifier (RA) plays a crucial role in determining the overall ADC performance. Closed-loop dynamic RA structures, such as ring amplifiers and floating inverter amplifiers (FIAs), have been actively researched for energy efficiency. Compared with ring amplifiers, FIAs offer inherently stable output common-mode (CM) voltage and attractive power efficiency owing to the self-quenching characteristic. However, pursuing high gain can limit the output swing, as seen in [3] due to the cascode last stage. A Miller-compensated two-stage FIA with a cascode 1st stage achieves wide output swing but is limited to a maximum DC gain of $\sim\left(\mathrm{g}_{m} \mathrm{ro}_{0}\right)^{3}$ [4]. Additionally, FIAs suffer from bandwidth limitations due to the self-quenching. Although ring amplifiers can be alternative choices for high speed [2], they consume static power [1], [2], [5].

articleTitle: A 0.0006-mm2 0.13-pJ/bit 9–21-Gb/s Sampling CDR with Inverter-Based Frequency Multiplier and Embedded 1:3 DEMUX in 65-nm CMOS
abstract: The growing demand for data throughput has led to the rapid development of serial I/O interfaces such as PCle, USB, and JESD204. As a key component, a compact and energy-efficient high-speed clock and data recovery (CDR) circuit is necessary. Figure 1 (top) shows the block diagram of the conventional CDR with a DFF-based phase detector (PD) and its severe flaws in tradeoffs among jitter, area, and retiming. To surmount these challenges, [1] proposes an inductor-less CDR utilizing a primary-secondary (P-S) sampler as the PD (Fig. 1, middle). In this way, the low-pass filter (LPF) is eliminated and a wide loop bandwidth is achieved, breaking the tradeoff between jitter generation and jitter tolerance (JTOL). However, due to the full-rate operation, high-speed rail-to-rail clocks are required. At extreme data rates, the power consumption for clock generation and distribution would increase sharply. Additionally, the inherent multi-phase clocks from the ring oscillator (RO) are used for retiming skew compensation, but the accuracy is pretty limited.

articleTitle: A Compact Low-power 16b SAR ADC using Reservoir-Charge-Redistributed DAC and Configurable Floating-Inverter-Based Comparator
abstract: Systems-on-chip applications have become imperative for high-precision ADCs with low power consumption and compact silicon area. SAR ADCs exhibit outstanding energy efficiency but necessitate high fidelity and fast settling reference voltages, often consuming considerable power and/or area. To alleviate such overheads, the passive-charge-sharing SAR ADCs have been reported [1] [2] [3], as shown in Fig.1. However, [1] suffers from a large reservoir capacitor (CREF) to capacitive DAC (CDAC) ratio of 80 for 14-bit resolution, and will further expand to 320 for 16 -bit. It also undergoes input-dependent bit weight errors and SNR degradation due to the shared bit capacitor (cap) and reference cap. While [2] [3] mitigates such constitutes by separating the bit and reference caps, its C<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">REF</inf>/C<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">DACC</inf> still limits to $\geq 8$, owing to the shrunken step size. This work proposes a reservoir-charge-redistributed SAR ADC that preserves the high SNR and linearity natures in [2] and decouples the compromise between the quantization step size and the value of $C_{\text {Ref }}$ in [2] [3], thus significantly suppressing the $C_{\text {ref/ }}$ dad $^{\prime}$ to 0.35 X A configurable floating inverter amplifier (FIA) -based comparator is also presented to improve the energy efficiency further and enable a regular 1.2 V supply implementation, which is different from 3.3 V in [1] [2] [3]. The ADC achieves an 80.9dB SNDR and 100.3dB SFDR at Nyquist input and consumes $291.7 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ power from a single supply at $1 \mathrm{MS} / \mathrm{s}$, yielding a $32.1 \mathrm{fJ} /$ conv.-step FoM<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">walden</inf> and 173.3 dB FoM<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">sch</inf>.

articleTitle: A Unified Microrobotic Visual-Perception Processor with 62.2-FPS/mm2 and 103-uJ/frame Navigation in 28nm
abstract: Microrobotic technology has made significant advancements recently, while the payload and power limitations restrict its development toward greater intelligence, for example, the constraint of $\sim 100 \mathrm{mg}$ and $\sim 100 \mathrm{~mW}$ in an insect-sized robot [1]. As an essential role in robotic navigation, visual perception usually has two critical components: localization and neural-network (NN) inference. The former has unique operators and dataflow featuring small-kernel filtering in the vision front-end (VFE) and, more importantly, the linear solver in the optimization back-end involves heavy Cholesky decomposition which is hard to cast into matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) [2]. These distinct dataflows usually lead to heterogeneous systems with separated fixed-function accelerators [3–7]. The visualinertial odometry in [3] focuses on localization and exploits fixedpattern sparsity in the back-end, which tradeoffs efficiency with restrictions on applications’ data distributions. The visual-perception SoCs in [5, 6] handle localization front-end and NN inference in robots efficiently, with the optimization back-end left external. However, severe system throughput degradation occurs when the computedemand ratio deviates from the native supply of the accelerators in diverse application scenarios [8], as shown in Fig. 1.

articleTitle: A 130-to-170 GHz Reconfigurable Heterodyne/Homodyne Transceiver Achieving 20.5-dBm Psat for Emerging Integrated Wireless Access and Backhaul Networks
abstract: Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) is an emerging wireless communication technology that combines wireless access and backhaul transmission within a single network infrastructure. As shown in Fig. 1, the IAB donor provides communication access to mobile users while handling wireless backhaul to IAB nodes via a wired connection to a data center. These IAB nodes then offer wireless access to users and manage backhaul traffic, acting as wireless relays to extend the coverage of the IAB donor. This setup is particularly beneficial in scenarios where line-of-sight (LoS) propagation is obstructed by obstacles like buildings. To support the evolving IAB network, the wireless transceiver must be reconfigurable between homodyne and heterodyne modes to address both backhaul and wireless access needs. However, current mm-wave/sub-THz transceivers typically use either zero-IF or heterodyne topologies, which are not ideal for the dynamic demands of IAB networks. This paper presents a 130-to-170GHz reconfigurable heterodyne/homodyne transceiver specifically designed for IAB networks. In homodyne mode, the transceiver facilitates data transfer between data centers and the IAB donor, while in heterodyne mode, it supports wireless connections between IAB nodes and users. Fabricated using 130nm SiGe technology, the transceiver achieves a measured saturated output power of 20.5 dBm, a minimum noise figure of 8.2 dB, and a 40 GHz bandwidth. Over-the-air (OTA) measurements confirm that the transceiver, operating in both modes, supports 16-QAM at 10 Gbps and 64-QAM at 3.6 Gbps, with corresponding EVM values of -15.7 dB and -23 dB. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a reconfigurable heterodyne/homodyne transceiver tailored for IAB networks.

articleTitle: A 428.4mW 6.78Mbps/3.61Mbps Up/Down Data Rate Wireless Chipset with TinyAI Regulation
abstract: Wireless power and data transmission (WPDT) systems that possess high power capability and efficiency as well as fast uplink/downlink data transmission (UDT/DDT) rate via single inductive link are in high demand for compact implants, such as cochlear, retinal prostheses and pacemaker for their increasingly advanced functionality and thermal safety. Conventionally, the load of the implanted RX-end needs to be monitored to either intermittently short the excessive power at the RX input for local regulation ($R X-L R$) or report the condition to the TX-end via UDT to correct the TX power for global regulation (TX-GR) [1] as in Fig. 1. $R X-L R$ is simple and fast but deteriorates the overall power efficiency which might cause rapid temperature rise while TX-GR improves the efficiency at the cost of UDT bandwidth. This design leverages a trained tiny artificial neural network (TinyAI) to extract the RX load condition solely from $V_{L}$ at the TX-end to timely adjust the TX power without UDT occupation nor excessive power shorting. In addition, a cyclic on-off-keying (COOK) with auto time tracking (ATT) and an adaptive encoded binary phase-shift keying (A-BPSK) are respectively proposed for UDT and DDT over the same inductive link at 13.56 MHz carrier frequency. The resulting $T X / R X$ chipset achieves 0.56% target regulation error, 3.7 X higher transmitted power and 1.4X higher DDT speed than prior arts.

articleTitle: A 273.48 TOPS/W and 1.58 Mb/mm2 Analog-Digital Hybrid CIM Processor with Transpose Ternary-eDRAM Bitcell
abstract: Deep neural network acceleration with Computing-in-Memory (CIM) processors [2–8] has been proposed to replace conventional computer architecture for high energy efficiency. However, previous CIM processors have struggled with the following limitations and challenges as shown in Fig. 1: 1) trade-off between cell density and computation linearity 2) trade-off between throughput degradation and analog-to-digital converter (ADC) area/power overheads, and 3) low system energy efficiency.

articleTitle: A Wireless Battery-Free Cerebral-Oxygen-Monitoring Micro-System Featuring 0.028% Sensing Resolution
abstract: Cerebral oxygen monitoring (COM) presents the partial pressure of oxygen $\left(\mathrm{PO}_{2}\right)$ in human brain, which helps with the treatment of various brain diseases such as traumatic brain injury (TBI). Longtermly COM can detect the potential cerebral hypoxia due to severe brain injuries, which is necessary in invasive medical treatment for TBI patients. To conduct accurate portable diagnosis in a long term, the COM devices are required to be wireless, high-resolution, long-lifetime, and miniature. Traditional PO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> sensing products such as Licox relied on bulk hardware and cables, which was not suitable for long-term portable monitoring. In recent years, plenty of researches try to change the bulky cable-based COM instruments into portable wireless devices, where low-power techniques are studied to extend the lifetime. As shown in Fig.1, there are two conventional PO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> sensing methods:1) Optical sensing method. A $4.5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ optical PO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> sensing device offered a resolution up to 0.09% [1], but the power-hungry LED driver limited the life time. For example, the LED driver consumed 20 mW power in [3], which presented to be the bottleneck in long-termly monitoring. 2) Electrochemical sensing. A resolution of $\pm 0.13 \%$ was achieved by a $42 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ cable-based electrochemical sensor [2]. Then, the PO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> sensing resolution was improved to 0.06% in [5], while it’s at the penalty of 1.4 mW power consumption due to the power-hungry trans-impedance amplifier (TIA). As a result, it’s difficult for the conventional COM devices to realize both a high resolution and a low power.

articleTitle: ANVMP: A 28nm 52.6 μW 1.25pJ/SOP Asynchronous Non- Volatile-Memory-based Computing-In-Memory Neuromorphic Processor for Edge-Al Applications
abstract: The increasing demand for low power edge-Al devices that target various tasks has driven many research efforts. To address this demand, many technologies such as computing-in-memory (CIM) [1], spiking neural networks (SNN) [2], and asynchronous logic [3] have been implemented on edge-Al devices. However, previous works either had energy consumptions of many mW [1, 2, 3, 5] or exclusively addressed a single task [4]. In this paper, we propose a neuromorphic processor (ANVMP) that adapts non-volatile memory (NVM)-based CIM, asynchronous logic and achieves the performance of $52.6~ \mu \text{W} 1.25 \text{pJ} / \text{SOP} \text{@} 0.55 ~\text{V}, 10 \%$ event rate, and $0.7 \%$ activation ratio (Fig. 1 (top)). The energy-efficient NVM-based CIM allows to power off the CIM macros completely during idle time to save power. The SNN-based neuromorphic computing uses binary coding which removes the need for DACs for CIM processing, and sparse spikes which reduce the energy consumption of information transmission with the cost of throughput. The event-driven nature of asynchronous logic allows energy to go where and when needed. Moreover, asynchronous logic offers fine-grained controls of CIM macros, which saves its power-on time.

articleTitle: A 24% Efficient, 15.36 dBm Output Power, Multi-Standard Digital Polar Transmitter with 7-bit Phase Interpolator-based BFSK Modulator and 23 dB Sidelobe Suppressed PA for Low-Power Wide Area Networks
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has become ubiquitous, permeating all areas of modern life. In low-power wide-area IoT networks, unfiltered BFSK modulation is often adopted due to its simple and low-power hardware despite occupying significant spectrum regions in multichannel communication environments [1]–[2]. The split-channel BFSK scheme addresses this trade-off by interleaving mark or space tones of additional channels $(\mathrm{CH} 1 / \mathrm{CH} 3)$ within the desired channel (CH2) [1]. While this approach results in an efficient utilization of frequency spectrum with BFSK modulation along with an improved RX BER performance, sidelobes from adjacent channels can serve as strong interferences, thereby deteriorating the signal-tointerference ratio (SIR). To improve the degraded SIR caused by the split-channel BFSK, this work proposes a sidelobe-suppressed digital PA that effectively reduces the undesired power levels in the sidebands by employing a triangular-enveloped waveform shaping to both the mark and space tones, resulting in 13 dB additional suppression to the first sidelobes as compared to conventional BFSK modulation. Additionally, to tackle the limited data rate challenge of PLL-based modulators, an open-loop, phase-interpolator (PI)-based phase-switching BFSK modulator is adopted. Integrating phase modulation from the BFSK modulator with amplitude modulation from the DPA, the proposed polar TX can be extended to accommodate multiple loT standards requiring complex modulation schemes like BPSK and QPSK.

articleTitle: A 300-GHz-Band 36-Gb/s Scalable 2x2 2D Phased-Array CMOS Receiver
abstract: Two-dimensional beamforming is a significant challenge for subterahertz transceivers. In this paper, we propose a two-dimensional beamforming receiver (RX) circuit that can be expanded to $n \times n$, and report the results of its $2 \times 2$ prototype implemented using 40 nm CMOS technology.

articleTitle: A 29.5W Switched-Capacitor based Dual-Output Hybrid Secondary Charger Providing Simultaneous Two-Cell Battery Charging and System Supply Voltage with Input Current Limiting Feature
abstract: The fast charging system for a two-cell battery typically consists of primary-secondary charging configurations followed by a buck converter to provide the system supply voltage (Vsys) [Fig. 1 (top)]. Recent works on efficient battery charging have focused on the primary charger capable of operating both as a voltage and current source [1] –[5]. By contrast, the secondary charger only needs to function as a current source, providing substantial charging current during the constant current (CC) mode. Among various secondary charger architectures, the 2:1 switched-capacitor (SC) power converter is highly favored due to its remarkable efficiency [6]. The SC converter can maintain a relatively constant charging current by adjusting the input voltage $\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{IN}}\right)$, relying on software communication between the USB input and the charger.

articleTitle: A 65nm 687.5-TOPS/W Drive Strength-based SRAM Compute-In-Memory Macro with Adaptive Dynamic Range for Edge AI applications
abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (ACIM) has been intensively investigated, pursuing better energy efficiency, network accuracy, and compatibility with various AI models [1–5]. In particular, SRAM-based ACIM macros achieve the flexibility of input/weight (IN/W) allocation incorporating bit-serial inputs, bitwise weight loading across multiple bitlines (BL), and digital shift-and-add multiplication of partial sum ($\mathrm{P}_{\text {sum }}$) in the output line (OL). However, shift-and-add multiplication inevitably exacerbates the $\mathrm{Psum}_{\text {sum }}$ errors arising from the computing/readout process under device mismatches and a limited sensing margin (SM) in ACIM (Fig. 1). This leads to severely erroneous MAC outputs and substantial accuracy loss, impeding the practical utilization of ACIM. To mitigate the Psum errors, the ACIM macro with high-precision IN/W and truncation at the MAC output was proposed [4]. The truncation filters out the quantization noise to an extent, thereby attaining the mitigated accuracy loss. Nevertheless, prior work still suffers from $\mathrm{P}_{\text {sum }}$ errors due to limited $V_{\text {LSB }}$ of high-resolution ADCs. Furthermore, the truncated MAC outputs undermine the advantages of high-precision IN/W undergoing frequent weight updates in ACIM macros. An alternative approach is using a low-resolution ADC with quantization for $\mathrm{P}_{\text {sum }}$ to secure higher $\mathrm{V}_{\text {LSB }}$ and suppress the resultant $\mathrm{P}_{\text {sum }}$ error [5]. However, under high macro utilization, it eventually suffers from accuracy loss due to quantization error, which is amplified by the shift and adder. To address the challenges, the drive strength-based SRAM compute-in-memory (DS-CIM) macro is proposed featuring: 1) $6 b$ drive strength-mode sensing with adaptive dynamic range that secures up to $39.2 x$-boosted sensing margin and 97% of error-free Psum readout on 2’s-complement 4b-IN/W ResNet-20 benchmarks, 2) row-wise adaptive dynamic range SAR (ADR-SAR) logic enabling concurrent ADC readout at every OL with the area efficiency of 15.83 TOPS $/ \mathrm{mm}^{2}, 3$) input-aware binary search (IABS) reducing average ADC conversion cycles by 64% on the ResNet-20 benchmark, and 4) a heterogeneous logic unit (HLU) for column-wise logic reconfigurability.

articleTitle: A 1kHz-to-62MHz 2.06zFrms Resolution Lock-in Amplifier with SAR-assisted Parasitic and Baseline Capacitance Compensation
abstract: The continuous advancement of sensing technology stimulates the demand for high-precision capacitive sensor interfaces for proximity detection, material analysis, and liquid level sensing. The capacitive transimpedance amplifier (C-TIA), based on lock-in sensing principle, can extract sub-fF level capacitance changes in an extremely noisy environment with balanced resolution and speed [1, 2]. However, there are still several design challenges in achieving ultra-high resolution down to zF levels. According to the equivalent capacitance noise equation in Fig.1, the parasitic capacitance $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{p}}$ at virtual ground is the first factor that limits the capacitance resolution before calibration. It also reduces the bandwidth and stability of the C-TIA. The second challenge is that the dynamic capacitance of interest $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{d}}$ often appears to be several orders of magnitude smaller than the inherent baseline value $\mathrm{C}_{\text {base }}$, calling for a large dynamic range to accommodate both types of capacitances, which imposes stringent requirements on the SNR. Another design challenge pertains to the DC bias of the C-TIA. Conventional pseudo-resistor (PR) for DC biasing is susceptible to significant resistance variation, and can easily saturate the TIA in the case of a nA-level leakage current from the sensor [3]. Although the DC servo loop (DSL) can solve this issue, conventional PR with fixed value still imposes significant constraints on the maximum input DC current. Moreover, the PR’s current noise, positively correlated to the input DC current, can dominant the CTIA’s noise performance [4, 5]. Additionally, addressing the system’s limitations with automatic calibration, rather than manual calibration, is crucial for increasing overall efficiency and user experience.

articleTitle: A 28nm 128-kb Exponent- and Mantissa-Computation-InMemory Dual-macro for Floating-point and INT CNNs
abstract: Floating point computation-in-memory (FP-CIM) has garnered significant attention in enhancing the energy efficiency of cloud and edge Al devices [1–3]. Recent advancements in large language models (LLM) and complex neural networks necessitate support for both floating point (FP) and integer (INT) multiplication-and-accumulation (MAC) operations to achieve superior performance and energy efficiency. Past FP-CIM implementations have utilized two primary methods for FP MAC operations: one involves utilizing extra exponent-mantissa alignment (EMA) and INT-FP quantization circuits, which necessitates offline data type conversion and isn’t considered true FP-CIM [1]. The other approach involves the use of additional exponent summation array and alignment circuits, enabling true FP-CIM but leading to increased area and energy consumption [2]. Efficiently implementing both true FP- and INTMAC operations can pose challenges for CIM macro. These challenges include: (a) the substantial area and energy overhead caused by extra exponent summation array (ESA) circuits when applied to INT MAC; (b) the significant power cost of readout circuits in previous analog or hybrid-domain CIM works; (c) the possibility of the aligned mantissa exceeding the maximum supported bit-precision of CIM size; and (d) the higher cost and power consumption of the larger adder tree in previous digital-domain CIM works, as shown in Fig. 1. This work presents a 28 nm 128kb exponent-computation-in-memory (ECIM) and mantissa-computation-in-memory (MCIM) dual-macro. The dual-macro can effectively support both true FP and INT MAC operations, offering the best energy efficiency (45.3 TFLOPS/W) in average case and the highest hardware utilization (>91.44%) for true-FP and INT configurations.

articleTitle: A 48MHz Temperature Compensated Crystal Oscillator Utilizing Time-Domain Accuracy Boosting Techniques Achieving ±1.4ppm Frequency Stability from -55°C to 115°C
abstract: Temperature Compensated Crystal Oscillators (TCXOs) are preferred over traditional XOs due to their capability to significantly reduce temperature’s impact on frequency stability. Adjusting load capacitance ($\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{L}}$) offers a straightforward and effective compensation method that integrates seamlessly into existing XOs without requiring additional reference sources or loops [1–5]. As depicted in Fig. 1, conventional analog compensation scheme processes temperature information directly in the voltage domain, ensuring a straightforward circuit implementation [4]. However, it faces challenges in compensation precision across process variations and adaptability for crystals with diverse temperature characteristics. In contrast, conventional digital compensation schemes convert temperature signals in a noiseless digital manner but may introduce transient frequency micro-jumps and parasitic spectra, potentially affecting phase noise (PN) due to the discrete-time refreshing and zero-order hold behavior of $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{L}}$ [1, 2, 3].

articleTitle: A 6.1fJ/conv-step 0.0017mm2 Level Crossing ADC for Compressive Neural Sensing with Event-Driven Ramp Generation and Sparse DAC Switching Scheme
abstract: This paper presents a dynamic level crossing ADC achieving a Walden FoM of $6.1 \mathrm{fJ} /$ conv-step and a data reduction of $\gt10 \times$ compared to conventional synchronous ADCs, while occupying an active area of only $0.0017 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. Asynchronous event generation within a low frequency clock period is exploited to significantly improve the energy efficiency without compromising in data reduction. To further improve energy efficiency, a novel DAC switching scheme optimized for sparse signals is presented. The presented LC-ADC supports 16 time-multiplexed neural sensing signals.

articleTitle: A 280.580 μm2/Grid, 30.7pJ TMRA-PIM (Time-Multiplexed Random-Access Processing-in-Memory) Programmable Accelerator for Partial Differential Equations Solving and Edge Processing
abstract: Hardware accelerators [1–3] employing processing-in-memory (PIM) techniques for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) using finite difference (FD) have received increasing attention thanks to their significant energy efficiency and low latency. However, a trilemma among density, programmability, and low latency hinders the practical use of such an accelerator. The accelerator must compromise its latency and programmability for better density. For instance, in addition to a lack of programmability, prior work in [2] enhances the density of [1] using a processing-near-memory architecture that compromises memory access latency. In contrast, a design in [3] utilized RISC CPU cores as programable processing elements (PEs) with a normalized area overhead $\gt300 \mathrm{x}$ of [2]. In this work, we propose a programmable PDE accelerator capable of both scientific computing and ultra-low power edge processing tasks such as trajectory error correction and pathfinding in robotics applications with minimized area and latency. A test chip with an $11 \times 22$ PE array is fabricated using a TSMC 40nm LP technology. Each PE performs instruction decode and execution via clock throttling, clock gating and data-path reconfiguration. Each executor within PE multiplexes between two memory groups featuring static and dynamic memory, maximizing area efficiency while preserving full functionality for PIM tasks including the ability to operate at a minimum frequency of 0.187 MHz. The test chip occupies a $0.1358 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ core area with a density of $280.580~ \mu \mathrm{m}^{2}$ per grid point, consumes $114.97~ \mu \mathrm{W}$ operating at $0.78 \mathrm{~V}, 3 \mathrm{MHz}$, and a 12 -bit computing precision.

articleTitle: A Real-Time Event Vision Sensor based Object Detection and Tracking System for Edge Applications
abstract: Recently, visual object detection and tracking (ODT) has become ubiquitous in intelligent edge platforms. RGB camera-based ODT systems using deep learning models [1] - [2] achieve high accuracy at the cost of significant power consumption. In contrast, event vision sensors (EVS) dramatically reduce the data volume, as events are generated only for moving objects. However, accurate object classification in event-based object tracking systems [5] – [7] is challenging due to the lack of detailed texture information. This paper proposes an energy-efficient ODT system that uses both the event stream and grayscale image from the EVS, featuring:1) A memory-efficient adaptive frame builder for event binary image (EBI) reconstruction without motion blur; 2) A memory-efficient region proposal unit for object localization with low latency; 3) A fully pipelined CNN engine with input sparsity enhancement and customized instruction set architecture (ISA).

articleTitle: A Hybrid Four-Switch Inductor-First Quadratic Step-Down Converter With Internal Ripple Compensated COT Control
abstract: With the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and the Internet of Things (loTs), the power demanded in data centers is growing rapidly. The power supply with an input voltage bus of 12 V or 24 V is widely used in data centers, while the supply voltages of the point-of-loads (PoL) have been reduced to 1 V due to the development of CMOS technology. Therefore, DC-DC converters with high voltage conversion ratio (VCR) and high efficiency are required. The converter with double step-down (DSD) [1]–[3] topology is proposed and the high VCR is achieved. However, the input current is not continuous and the Electro-Magnetic Interference (EMI) is large. Furthermore, the loss of the direct current resistance (DCR) is large in the topology that the inductor is directly connected to the load as shown in Fig. 1 (top left). Fig. 1 (top middle) shows that the DCR loss can be reduced up to 50% by using inductor-first (IF) topology. However, the conventional inductor-first topology shown in Fig. 1 (top right) is not suitable for the high voltage conversion application.

articleTitle: A 33.6nW Capacitively Coupled Chopper Amplifier with Stacked Input-Boosted Gate-and-Bulk-Driven Inverter Achieving 0.59 NEF and 0.42 PEF in 180nm CMOS
abstract: The overall noise in a sensor read-out circuit is typically dominated by the front-end-amplifier. Achieving low noise often requires high power due to the inherent tradeoff between transconductance $G_{m}$ and bias current $I_{d}$ of the transistor. Developing techniques to mitigate this noise-power tradeoff is crucial for power- and energy-constrained systems. Inverter-based amplifier can effectively double the $G_{m} / I_{d}$ ratio through two-fold current reuse. In [1], the input-boosted inverter-based amplifier achieved both current reuse and input boosting simultaneously, resulting in a four-fold improvement in $G_{m} / I_{d}$. Stacking amplifiers can further increase the ratio of current reuse, with one design achieving six-fold current reuse and a corresponding six-fold boost in $G_{m} / I_{d}$ [2]. However, the power-consuming current summation branch reduces the power efficiency. Inserting AC-coupling capacitors at the outputs of the stacked amplifier can eliminate the current summation branch, and a ten-fold gm/ld boosting was reported [3]. Despite these advancements, the supply voltage of the stacking structure increases with the number of stacking stages, which impedes further improvement in the power-efficiency factor (PEF). This work introduces a 3-stacking topology with six-fold current reuse using an input-boosted gate-and-bulk-driven inverter-based amplifier, effectively increasing $G_{m}$ and the number of stacking stages for a given power budget. Fabricated in $0.18 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ CMOS, the proposed capacitively coupled chopper instrumentation amplifier (CCIA) achieves an integrated input-referred-noise (IRN) of $2.16 \mu \mathrm{Vrms}$ within a bandwidth of 550 Hz, resulting in a noise-efficiency factor (NEF) and PEF of 0.59 and 0.42, respectively. Compared to the CCIA with an input-boosted inverter-based amplifier [1], the NEF and PEF are improved by approximately 40% and 27%, respectively. Even compared to a topology with ten-fold current reuse [3], the NEF and PEF are enhanced by about 31% and 57%, respectively, with only six-fold current reuse.

articleTitle: A 16nm 231mW Channel MLP Optimized Neural Processing Unit for 80.3% Top-1 ImageNet Classification Accuracy at 102fps
abstract: Channel multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) is playing a crucial role in today’s neural networks, such as Transformer. Furthermore, MetaFormer [5] demonstrates that with separated channel MLPs, simply using pooling layers as spatial token mixers (i.e. PoolFormer, PF) exhibit exceptional performance as well, as shown in Fig. 1. Despite the advantage in terms of complexity and accuracy, we identify three design challenges for efficient deployment on edge devices. Firstly, massive external memory access (EMA) is induced due to the channel expansion in MLP blocks. Secondly, processing throughput could be degraded by the computation latency of feature statistics for layer norm (LN) and the low MAC utilization for a largekernel CONV $7 \times 7$ layer. Thirdly, classification accuracy could be degraded by fixed-point implementation for LN and Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU). In this work, we present a high-performance processor to address the challenges with three key features:1) EMA reduction with bottleneck-based layer fusion (BBLF) and model-divided batch mode (MDBM) for MLP; 2) throughput improvement with LN pipelined scheduling (LNPS) and kernel reshaping (KRS) for CONV77;× 3) complexity-efficient and accuracy-preserved fixed-point LN and difference-LUT-based GELU.

articleTitle: A 45-fsrms Accumulated Jitter PLL Using Advanced Design Techniques for PCIe Gen6 Reference Clock Generation in 2 nm MBCFET Technology
abstract: The continuous advancement of technology has led to the increase in data rates of high-speed serial links like PCIe, MPHY, USB and Ethernet, with stringent random jitter (RJ) specifications. The PCIe protocol, for instance, necessitates a reference clock frequency of 100 MHz for its Tx/Rx PLLs and CDR. To achieve this, a temperature-compensated crystal oscillator (TXCO) with low jitter can be used, but it incurs additional overhead on power (to drive the TXCO) and area (increase in number of soldier balls for flip-chip integration), thereby escalating production costs [1]. An alternative is to use an on-chip dedicated low-jitter PLL with tens of MHz of TXCO (low-cost). The system-on-chip (SoC) needs a fast lock time for this PLL, so it should support fast bring-up to meet PCIe compliance requirements. The SoC environment is also known for its severe temperature drift, which can reach up to $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and more. In automotive applications, the PLL requires even wider range of temperature drift, compared to mobile applications. In addition, the absence of thick-oxide devices in 2 nm middle bridge-channel FET (MBCFET) technology poses a design challenge for high-performance analog blocks powered by 1.2 V supply. To overcome these challenges, we propose a low-jitter PLL for PCIe reference clock generation that includes optimization techniques for low jitter and low area. A reliability-aware analog design approach for 1.2 V tolerant designs and a fast-locking scheme based on fully-synthesizable, digital bang-bang automatic frequency calibration (AFC) are presented. Also, advanced layout techniques are suggested to achieve the tracking capability of the on-chip temperature drift. The proposed PLL is fabricated in 2 nm MBCFET technology with an active area of $0.048 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$, and it achieves a 45-$\mathrm{fS}_{\mathrm{r} m \mathrm{~m}}$ accumulated jitter for the PCIe-Gen6 application, a dynamic temperature range (DTR) of $-45^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a lock time of $6 \mu \mathrm{~s}$.

articleTitle: PRIM-CAEFA: A 64K-spin Packet-based Reconfigurable Ising Machine with Cross-problem Adjustment-free Energy Feedback Annealing
abstract: Ising machine is designed to solve optimization problems. State-of-the-art CMOS Ising machines [1] –[7] are divided into two types: all-to-all interaction and sparse interaction (Fig. 1 top). The former type is more desirable for solving a variety of problems with complex interaction patterns, but it suffers from performance and hardware resources scalability issue [2], [5]. In contrast, the sparse degree (number of interactions) of the latter type leads to better performance and scalability [1], [3] –[5], [7], however, without minor embedding (extra mapping effort, degraded accuracy, replica spins), the limited degree results in limited applicable problem sets. e-Chimera [1] and Flexible spin processing elements [3] enlarge the flexibility of sparse interaction Ising machines, yet the problems that can be solved by machine with limited number of graph topologies [1] or fixed degree global interactions [3] are still less than the all-to-all interaction machine; all-to-all interaction is more desirable for a variety of optimization problems. Latch-based circuits are suitable for implementing all-to-all interaction. However, due to the deterministic property of latch, external annealing algorithms, which require tedious adjustment of the hyperparameters for each problem, should be implemented. To leverage the advantages of two types Ising machine and avoid the time-consuming hyperparameter adjustment, we propose a Packet-based Reconfigurable Ising Machine (a spin includes the spin itself and packets, where the packet includes the characteristics of spin) with Cross-problem Adjustment-free Energy Feedback Annealing (PRIM-CAEFA) (Fig. 1 bottom), featuring 1) reconfigurable and scalable a) spin number (up to 64 K within one chip) and b) interaction number (all-to-all interaction for versatile applications, sparse random interaction for adaptable computation and performance); the global sparse random degree is suitable for solving all kinds of problem without extra mapping effort, redundant computation or area consuming. 2) only 10 iterations to reach 90% of the minimum energy. 3) general usage annealing without tedious adjustment of the hyperparameters. 4) the capability of solving integer factorization on CMOS Ising machine.

articleTitle: A TFT-Based Flexible PPG Acquisition Circuit in a 3-μm LTPS Process for Packaging-Free Smart Ring Applications
abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a commonly used non-invasive biological signal detection technique that can analyze the heart rate and blood oxygen saturation, which plays an important role in daily health monitoring. In Fig. 1 (top), integrating biological acquisition into smart rings is an emerging trend in the consumer electronics [1]. However, integrating all building blocks into a space-limited device encounters challenges. It also bring discomfort to the users. A feasible integrate solution is soldering Si chips onto a flexible substrate which requires costly packaging [2]. The semi flexible system constrains its bendability, still requiring an extensive dynamic range (DR) to mitigate motion artifacts [3].

articleTitle: A 32×32 SPAD LiDAR Sensor with In-pixel Spatial-temporal Coincidence and Per-SPAD Pulse Delay for Resolution-lossless Imaging
abstract: Single-photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD)-based LiDAR technology finds significant applications in advanced driver assistance systems, etc. Extracting distance information necessitates creating a histogram from enormous frames to filter out the overwhelming background light (BGL) data. As the formats of SPAD pixel arrays scaling up [1], the processing, storage, and transmission of extensive data result in ultra-high power consumption and increased layout area. In order to reduce BGL, previous studies [2][3] [4] have leveraged spatial coincidence and histograms in pixels, and [5] utilized external double pulses to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. However, a significant amount of data still needs to be processed within the sensor. To address these challenges, this paper presents a $32 \times 32$ SPAD LiDAR sensor that incorporates in-pixel spatial-temporal coincidence to effectively compress random background light and a per-SPAD pulse delay method to realize resolution-lossless imaging. This approach achieves an impressive 98.3% compression rate of background light under 100 klux illumination while maintaining a low power consumption of $14.6 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ per pixel.

articleTitle: A 14-to-32-Gb/s Deadzone-Free Referenceless CDR with Autocovariance-based Frequency Detector in 40-nm CMOS Technology
abstract: As data rate continues to rise in wireline communications, high-speed and low-cost clock and data recovery (CDR) has become a crucial part of receiver design [1]–[6]. The referenceless CDR has been explored to reduce hardware costs while maintaining wide-range operation because it does not require an external clock source. However, referenceless CDR should address several challenges. Since it does not receive synchronization information with the incoming data, the referenceless CDR should extract the corresponding frequency relying only on the data sequence. To achieve a wide and fast transient response, we adopt the stochasticbased FD (SFP) concept [1]. By collecting three consecutive data sequences and processing them correctly in Figs. 1(a), (b), and (c), the SFD shows remarkable locking behavior. However, in specific loop gain settings, they sometimes fall into the wrong frequencies and cannot escape that deadzone. Therefore, this manuscript thoroughly investigates when and why the deadzone occurs, and the new concept of autocovariance is introduced to prevent false locking.

articleTitle: An 8-bit 20.2fJ/conv-step FoM CI-C Asynchronous SAR ADC with Common-mode Level Shifting
abstract: With the recent widespread adoption of DSP-based Serdes and process-in-memory (PIM) technologies, the demand for energy-efficient ADCs with small area and moderate resolution ($5-8$ bits) has increased significantly. For high energy efficiency of ADCs, CDAC-based SAR ADCs have been commonly used, but they are limited in reducing the core area. To improve this, a charge-injection (CI) cell based SAR (CI SAR) ADC [1] was proposed demonstrating high speed of $1 \mathrm{GS} / \mathrm{s}$ and a small core area, but it not only increases the input load due to the large input capacitance, but also has poor linearity due to the common-mode voltage $\mathrm{V}_{\text {cm }}$ variation accompanying the conversion progress, which limits the input signal range narrowly. A 6-bit CI SAR ADC [2] has been proposed to achieve high linearity with a small sampling capacitor while enhancing PVT robustness. This structure applies bias voltage compensation using a replica ADC, and it can shift $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{CM}}$ during the conversion. However, different capacitor metals on the p-side and n side are used for small capacitor area, which can affect the linearity at higher resolutions than 6-bit.

articleTitle: A 31.92% Efficiency Colpitts DCO-PA for BLE TX with Implicit RX Clock Generation Using DM-to-CM Mode-switching
abstract: Ultra-low-power (ULP) transceivers (TRX) play a crucial role in Internet of Things (IoT) applications, where Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is currently the most popular low-power short-range communication protocol [1–6]. In a conventional TX (Fig. 1(a)), considerable power is consumed into PA driving stages (Pdc,Drive), primarily an RF oscillator and possibly a frequency divider plus buffers in cascading stages, which cannot scale with output $P_{\text {RF }}$ and thus limit the system efficiency. Function-reuse DCO-PAs [1, 3] (Fig. 1(b)) are proposed to merge the driving capability of the RF oscillator into the PA making it self-driven, thereby reducing the Pdc,Drive for scalability and efficiency. However, there are still unsolved issues with recent DCO-PAs: (1) The DCO-PA [1, 3] cannot generate the local oscillator (LO) signal for RX resulting from the inevitable antenna leakage due to the simultaneous power-on of oscillating and PA when directly utilized DCO-PA in RX mode; (2) The source-to-gate transformer (xfmr)-feedback DCO-PA [1] exhibits low efficiency owing to unexpected source swing limiting drain peak output.

articleTitle: A 5.76GS/s 180MHz-BW 74.1dB-DR 2x TI Extrapolated CT DSM with Broadband Hybrid-Inputs Current-Mode Adder in 28nm CMOS
abstract: In recent years, Gigahertz-rate oversampled CT DSMs have been consistently explored to pursue a larger bandwidth (BW) [1] –[4]. Note that the usable oversampling ratio (OSR) is seriously limited (i.e. below 10) in those works owing to the restrained clock rate. A low OSR results in poor quantization efficiency, thus limiting the achievable dynamic range (DR). In such an ultra-low-OSR context, multi-stage noise-shaping (MASH) topology [2–3] can achieve $\sim 70 \mathrm{~dB}$ DR at 360 MHz and 465 MHz BWs, respectively. However, those broadband MASH CT DSMs significantly suffer from quantization noise (QN) leakage, requiring digital calibrations, which consume large power and area.

articleTitle: ROC-Spin: A 28nm 2,000 Ring-Oscillator-Collapse Spins for Solving Combinatorial Optimization Problems
abstract: Emerging computer based on quantum [1] or CMOS technologies [2 –5] has gained attention as an alternative for solving non-deterministic polynomial-time hard combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) intractable using classical computers. Among them, oscillator-based Ising chips [3–4] demonstrated cost-effective, massively parallel, scalable, and energy efficient solutions. Such Ising chips implemented a two-dimensional (2-D) array of spins through a network of coupled ring oscillators where their spin states are represented by the oscillation phases. The oscillator-based spins naturally find their minimum energy states, where the oscillators are synchronized to the same (in-phase) or the opposite (out-of-phase) oscillation phase. However, the phase-based spin interactions could degrade the accuracy of solutions due to a complex phase readout circuitry, which is prone to errors, and lead to a significant hardware overhead. To mitigate these issues, this work proposes a novel ring-oscillator-collapse (ROC) spin circuit, where a duty cycle of its output clock represents spin state. For instance, a 100% duty-cycle (or DC high) represents spin-up, a 0% duty-cycle (DC low) represents spin-down. A duty cycle between 0% and 100% represents a superposed state, which will eventually collapses to either a DC high (spin-up) or low (spin-down) as a result of interactions between ROC spins. The collapsed spin states (a DC high or low) are read out using a simple digital read circuit with minimal error and area overhead. A 28 nm test chip with 2,000 ROC spins demonstrated 0.1% error rate and $3-50 \mathrm{~ns}$ time-to-solution (TTS) for solving max-cut problems.

articleTitle: A 24.25–29.5-GHz Transmitter with Built-in Automatic Calibration of LO Feedthrough and I/Q Imbalance in 65-nm CMOS
abstract: Due to the vast spectra and low latency, millimeter-wave 5 G wireless communication networks have become highly attractive. The 24.25-$29.5-\mathrm{GHz}$ band has been allocated as one of the 5 G new radio (NR) frequency range 2 (FR2) operating bands (i.e., n257, n258, n261). To achieve low error vector magnitude (EVM) in these bands, it is crucial to mitigate local oscillator feedthrough (LOFT) and I/Q imbalance. Compared with traditional methods, built-in automatic calibration for LOFT suppression and image rejection offers significant advantages for fast mass production.

articleTitle: A 3-D Ising Machine with 12-Way Supply-and-Bulk Injection Locking Oscillators for Combinatorial Problem Solving
abstract: Ising machine is an emerging quantum-inspired computing processor that quickly solves the combinatorial problem. Compared to quantum computers, CMOS Ising machine searches the ground or approximate lowest Hamiltonian energy at room temperature with much lower power consumption and a smaller form factor [1] –[7], [9], [10]. Nevertheless, the state-of-the-art CMOS Ising machine still faces challenges for solving real-world problems.

articleTitle: A 0.91-pJ/b 20.8–32-Gb/s Reference-Less Sub-Baud-Rate CDR Circuit
abstract: Clock and data recovery (CDR) circuits are widely used in multi-standard transceivers. To improve the energy efficiency of 2 x oversampling phase detectors (PDs) in digital CDR circuits, a baud-rate PD [1], and sub-baud-rate PDs [2]–[4] are presented to reduce the required number of sampling clock phases and clock buffers. Some CDR circuits use frequency detectors (FDs) [1], [3] to extend the frequency capture range (FCR) in multi-standard applications. However, additional slicers or hardware are required, which degrade the energy efficiency. In this work, a sub-baud-rate reference-less CDR circuit using six slicers and an active differentiator is presented to improve energy efficiency. Since the number of slicers is reduced, the output capacitive load of the continuous-time linear equalizer (CTLE) is improved. To extend the CTLE’s bandwidth, an active inductor and a negative capacitor are used. A sub-baud-rate FD is also realized by sharing the slicers of the sub-baud-rate PD.

articleTitle: A 28nm 118.26TOPS/W Multi-Dimensional Fault-Tolerant Al Processor Enabling Voltage-Frequency Scaling Below Point-of-First-Failure
abstract: Al algorithms have succeeded tremendously, while the tremendous power from data access and computing prevents their applications [1–5]. Generally, AI computing comprises iterative memory access, sparsity processing, and MAC operations. Specifically, Al processors in each cycle fetch sparse operands from SRAM and compress nonzero data into a dense format for MAC computing. These three steps consume $\sim 90 \%$ of power. Adaptive voltage-frequency scaling (AVFS) can dynamically adjust voltage based on point-of-first-failure (PoFF). It is a promising method to achieve quadratic power saving. However, the conventional AVFS incurs severe accuracy degradation even with slight MSB errors, limiting the VF scaling boundary. 1) SRAM incurs random compulsory “0” or “1” bit errors under low voltage. Only 0.03% of errors in MSBs affect the accuracy by 29.2%. (2) The sparsity processing suffers timing violations at a low voltage. Once 1.3% of violations at the MSBs of large values occur, the accuracy decreases by 22.8%. (3) The MAC unit undergoes MSB faults at low voltage due to the LSB-to-MSB carry propagation logic, where 0.01% MSB errors degrade accuracy by 43.9%.

articleTitle: A 56Gbps ADC/DAC-Based Jitter-Robust Multicarrier Transceiver with RX MIMO-DSP for > 40dB Loss Channel
abstract: Clock jitter places fundamental performance limitations on ADC/DAC-based wireline transceivers that utilize conventional baseband amplitude modulation signaling. Alternative signaling schemes that utilize a combination of baseband and up-converted multiple carriers allow for additional coherent (amplitude/phase) modulation and provide longer symbol times to improve jitter robustness. However, channel dispersion causes both inter-symbol interference (ISI) and inter-channel interference (ICI) between signaling bands. Previous multicarrier signaling architectures have utilized relatively large carrier spacings to minimize ICI, resulting in poor spectral efficiency [1], or utilized tightly-space orthogonal carriers and performed simple off-chip ICl cancellation that only allows for operation over moderate loss channels [3]. In this work, a $56 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ multicarrier transceiver is demonstrated that enables the use of tightly-space orthogonal carriers for high-loss channels with 40.8 dB insertion loss by introducing a RX MIMO-DSP that efficiently cancels both ISI and ICI with five 5-tap FIR filters for each of the baseband, mid-band I/Q, and high-band I/Q channels compared to the work in [2] [3].

articleTitle: A 400 × 112 CMOS LiDAR Sensor with Reconfigurable-Resolution Histogramming Time-to-Digital Converters and Sub-cm Depth Refining Filter
abstract: For long-range scan light detection and ranging (LiDAR), two parameters are crucial: spatial and time resolution. Because target objects located at far distances provide only a few points on a low resolution sensor, higher spatial resolution is essential. For mechanical LiDAR, which achieves high resolution through mechanical laser scanning, increased scanning leads to lower frame rate. Moreover, a large form factor and low manufacturability can be problematic [1]. A solid-state LiDAR with row-addressable laser scanning overcame the shortcomings of mechanical LiDAR. However, achieving high resolution remains challenging due to the dense column-parallel histogramming time-to-digital converters (hTDCs) in small pitch. Even though a QVGA sensor has been reported, only the pixels, not hTDC, are reconfigured to achieve high resolution, hTDCs that can be accessed per laser emission is limited to half of the horizontal image resolution [2]. Therefore, the resolution of state-of-the-art sensors is below $200 \times 100$ [3], [4]. The time resolution is also crucial for identifying objects in a three-dimensional way. Unfortunately, owing to the limited capacity of the histogram memory, low time resolution over $1-\mathrm{ns}(15-\mathrm{cm})$ was allowed.

articleTitle: A 22T Static Contention-free Conjoined Master-Slave Flip-flop for Low-Voltage, Low-Power, and Low-Area Applications
abstract: Low-voltage flip-flops that operate reliably in a low-voltage regime are crucial for extending battery life in energy-constrained IoT applications. Minimizing dynamic power consumption is also vital for reducing overall SoC power. Additionally, it is important to reduce the area occupied by flip-flops as a significant portion of processor area is dedicated to sequential elements. Prior-art flip-flop designs [1–6] have aimed to be static contention-free (for robustness) and eliminate redundant clock transitions (for low power) simultaneously. However, many failed to meet one of these goals [1–4] or achieved both at a high area cost. This paper introduces a novel design that meets both requirements and achieves a smaller area compared to a conventional Transmission Gate Flip-Flop (TGFF) design.

articleTitle: Similarity-Aware Transposable SRAM Computation-In-Memory with Pulse-Based SAR ADC
abstract: Computation-in-memory (CIM) is a promising approach that aims to improve the energy efficiency in calculating the multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) of deep neural networks (DNNs) by performing computations directly in memory. However, the data-driven feature has not been explored enough, which could drastically improve energy efficiency. LowMAC first [7] and SS-SAR hybrid CIM [8] have been proposed considering bell-shaped MAC, but those works have a high detection fail rate as they did not consider statistical information such as correlation. This work found a high correlation between the preceding and the current MAC result due to the overlap of the convolutional window, as shown in Fig. 1 (top-left). This paper proposes similarity-aware CIM (SA-CIM) with three features: 1) similarity-aware ADC (SA-ADC) to exploit convolutional similarity, leading to a 31.5% ADC power reduction, 2) capacitor-based transposable bitcell, improving linearity and symmetricity, 3) pulse-based ADC to overcome dual ADC area overhead of transposable CIM, leading to 44.4% transistors reduction.

articleTitle: A 1.12nJ/Pixel High-Accuracy and Memory-Efficient Real-Time Object Detection Processor for Neuromorphic Vision Sensors
abstract: Neuromorphic vision sensors (NVSs) [1], which generate an event only when a pixel’s log intensity changes, feature low data redundancy and transmission latency, making them increasingly popular in various edge applications, such as traffic monitoring and object detection. Compared to event-by-event processing paradigms that require the processor to be always-on [2], frame-based counterparts are more power-efficient, as they keep the processor in an idle state during frame construction, resulting in a reduced signal toggling rate. However, as NVSs continue to evolve, the increasing resolution necessitates a substantial amount of on-chip memory to hold the reconstructed event-based binary image (EBBI), as depicted in Fig. 1 (top). Furthermore, most existing systems are suited only for stationary scenes, as moving NVSs introduce background noise [3]. In addition, prior object detection systems based on deep neural networks (DNN) or connected component labeling (CCL) suffer from significant memory overhead and long processing latency due to large model sizes and high computational intensity.

articleTitle: A 0.9V CMOS Voltage Reference with 0.41% Untrimmed Accuracy and 44.7 ppm/°C TC from -35°C to 130°C
abstract: A stable bandgap voltage reference (BGR) with low power consumption and small area is essential for the long-term operation and miniaturization of Internet-of-Things sensors and implantable devices. Recently, CMOS-only circuits [1] –[4] have been proposed to meet this requirement. However, when using the threshold voltage $\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{TH}}\right)$ of MOSFETs as a complementary-to-absolute-temperature (CTAT) voltage ($\mathrm{V}_{\text {CTAT}}$) in a reference, the inherent variability of $\mathrm{V}_{\text {TH}}$ would introduce process dependency. To compensate the process variation in $\mathrm{V}_{\text {TH,}}$, a hybrid architecture combining BGR and CMOS reference with dimension-induced side effects [5] has been proposed. Nevertheless, the compensation relies on a BJT-generated proportional to faster-skewed process (PTFP) voltage (VPTFP), constraining the minimum supply voltage to 1 V. Alternatively, [1] utilizes the threshold difference between transistors in stacked diode MOS transistors (SDMT) to generate an output that is robust to PVT variations without using BJTs, effectively reducing the supply voltage to 0.9 V. Nonetheless, since Vctat and Vptap are generated within the same SDMT, individual optimization of TC curvature without affecting process compensation is complicated, resulting in a high temperature coefficient (above $60 \mathrm{ppm} /{}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$) from -40 to $130^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. This paper presents a compensation method that eliminates the use of BJT by separating PTAT and CTAT generators from a single branch. The proposed technique introduces VPTFP to the output through the $\vee_{\text {TH}}$ difference of the input transistor pair within the PTAT-embedded amplifier, while enhancing Vctat linearity with a nonlinear CTAT current. Fabricated in 180nm CMOS, the untrimmed voltage reference exhibits a 0.4% standard deviation and a TC of $44.7 \mathrm{ppm} /{}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ from $-35^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $130^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, with a mean output of 524 mV.

articleTitle: A 174nW Event-Driven Keyword Spotting ASIC with DC-Drift-Resilient Dual-Mode Delta/SAR Quantizer and Multiplier-Less Processor
abstract: Recently, significant progress has been achieved in low-power keyword spotting (KWS) ASICs, which can serve as always-on wake-up function blocks for computationally intensive speech processing tasks. A 3-class CNN based KWS classifier consumed 510 nW power without including on-chip ADCs [1]. In [2], an ultra-low power event-driven level-crossing (LC) ADC was employed, reducing standby power to 148 nW. However, LC-ADC is vulnerable to DC drift. Other works include a 12-class KWS chip consuming $23 \mu \mathrm{~W}$ power [3], and a skip RNN-based 7-class KWS chip consuming 1.5 $\mu \mathrm{W}$ power [4]. Despite these technological advancements, researchers are still seeking KWS solutions with even lower power consumption, while not compromising on other key specifications such as keyword variety, classification accuracy and latency.

articleTitle: A 3-to-40 GHz 64QAM/256QAM/4096QAM Zero-IF CMOS Transceiver Chipset for Millimeter-wave Software-defined Radios
abstract: The widely available frequency spectrum at the millimeter-wave (mm-Wave) band can be adopted to achieve high-speed wireless communication in Wi-Fi, cellular, and wireless backhaul systems While there are extensive research, development, and demonstration of mm-Wave systems, the software-defined radios (SDRs) for mm-Wave, which offer flexibility, adaptability, and cost-efficiency, are still very much in its infancy as compared to the SDR for sub-6 GHz. A major challenge for the mm-Wave SDR is the lack of low-cost and portable mm-Wave transceivers covering sub-GHz to several tens of GHz frequency range continuously. Authors in [1]–[3] demonstrate ultra-wideband mm-Wave front-ends for phased-array systems using SiGe technology with high cost and low integration level. A 0.3-to-40 GHz receiver (RX) [4] and a 24-to-71 GHz RX [5] using CMOS technology are reported. However, only few ultra-wideband RXs with larger than 150% fractional bandwidth are published and there is no ultra-wideband CMOS TX and RX chipset for mm-Wave SDRs reported in open literature so far. To demonstrate the possibility and feasibility of transceivers for mmWave SDRs, this paper introduces a 64QAM/256QAM/1024QAM 4096QAM zero-IF 3-to-40 GHz TX and 0.03-to-40 GHz RX chipset in CMOS technology. In addition, several ultra-wideband RF/mm-wave circuit design challenges in the building blocks are addressed. This paper demonstrates the completely fully functional TX-to-RX link with a data rate of $7.2 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ with outstanding measured system performance based on the proposed transceiver chipset.

articleTitle: A 1.06V 5Gb/s/pin 16Gb LPDDR4x DRAM Adopting Sense Amplifier with AC-Coupled Equalizer, Stacked Output Driver, and Clock MUX with Inverter-Based Transmission Gate for Mobile and Automotive Application
abstract: For increasing consumers’ needs for processing data at high speed and low power consumption in mobile devices and automotive applications, LPDDR DRAMs have been much more challenged and struggled for achieving high data bandwidth without increasing power consumption. To meet these trends, many papers like [1], [2] have introduced new I/O circuitry techniques for LPDDR DRAMs because I/O circuitry is one of major points for achieving not only low power consumption but also high data bandwidth. This paper proposes new I/O schemes: a sense-amplifier with AC-coupled equalizer (ACCE), a stacked output driver, and a duty-immune clock multiplexer (CLKMUX). The ACCE enhances a write (WR) I/O margin while minimizing an increase of input capacitance during the WR operation. And the stacked output driver improves a read (RD) I/O margin reducing a power consumption during the RD operation. Finally, the CLKMUK also increases a RD I/O margin by removing an effect of duty variations on internal clock. By adopting the proposed I/O schemes, the measured WR I/O margin is improved by 28% and the RD I/O margin also improved by 20% with reducing the power consumption of 21% compared to the previous LPDDR4/4x DRAM products.
